item.title: State Of The Tech Job Market: Late 2026
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
State Of The Tech Job Market: Late 2026

Lenny Rachitsky

Here’s what we’re seeing right now: (1) PMs seem to be winning in the AI era. (2) Engineering demand has stalled. (3) Design is at a record low. (4) Everybody now needs to AI. (5) Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area. (6) Remote is at a record low. (7) The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!)

#Survey Career IndustryTrends

item.title: New Units Of Knowledge
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
New Units Of Knowledge

Kevin Kelly

“In the past, books were the primary unit of knowledge. When computers came along, knowledge was combined with action, and the shareable unit became software code. The web made the page and the link the unit, and for twenty years knowledge spread hyperlink by hyperlink. Code itself became shareable as packages and libraries that anyone could snap together. Later, mobile phones refined the knowledge unit into the “app.” Tremendous amounts of potential knowledge and action are compressed into a tiny app, which can be shared, bought, and sold.”

#History IndustryTrends

👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

The Pulse: What can we learn from the Railway hack?

Also: native mobile and frontend jobs are disappearing, how trust helps an “AI-native” engineering team to succeed, Carta starts selling a coding harness, and more

Gergely Orosz
Nov 12
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover:

  1. What can we learn from the Railway hack? Cloud platform Railway has published an extremely detailed postmortem about their recent hack in which the attacker likely used ‘abliterated’ AI models (those with no safeguards). Railway has hardened its systems as a result. Also, a competitor tried to benefit from the incident by getting Railway’s customers to migrate – but then got hacked itself in the exact same way.

  2. Native mobile and frontend jobs are disappearing. New data shows native mobile and frontend job listings are down by 50% at leading startups and Big Tech, while forward deployed engineer (FDE) listings have quadrupled in the same timeframe.

  3. How an extremely efficient engineering team works: Superlogical. Mitchell Hashimoto’s new startup is “AI-native” and cares deeply about craft and developer tools. They skip code reviews and commit to main thanks to deep trust between team members.

  4. Industry pulse. Jensen Huang no longer the CEO of NVIIDA, OpenAI buys Pierre Computer, Carta starts selling a coding harness, Meta buys and shuts down Conductor (a T3Code competitor), and Binance hacked with $6.3B stolen after devs were tricked into downloading packages and attending fake interviews.

1. What can we learn from the Railway hack?

Over the past two weeks I’ve talked with several CTOs and founders at infra companies, and in those circles, it’s an open secret that companies are being targeted by what looks like Chinese attackers, using abliterated AI models (those with no safeguards). These attackers seem to only want AI model keys; most likely to sell at discounted rates. “Popping” an infra company and accessing thousands of AI keys can be profitable, so it’s economical to spend heavily on offensive abliterated models.

Cloud provider Railway was one of the several infra providers that was hacked two weeks ago, with customer secrets leaked. The company has released a very detailed postmortem, which is the most in-depth description of how such an attack happens and how fast attackers adapt.

At a high level, this is what happened:

  • Phase #1: Several unsuccessful exploit attempts. On 18 Oct, the attacker created dummy Railway accounts and tried unsuccessfully to get into the company’s systems. The attacks are blocked, but the attacker did not give up.

  • Phase #2: Get Railway’s monorepo code (5 steps in 11 hours). The steps:

    • Attacker finds a vulnerability so they can read files on Railway’s build system

    • → steals build credentials

    • → tries the credentials on several internal systems

    • → accesses a Temporal cluster that stores build histories

    • → finds Railway’s monorepo as a build history and downloads it

  • Phase #3: Gain SSH access to Railway’s cloud environment (4 steps in 10 hours):

    • Scans the downloaded code; tries using old endpoints

    • → Gets a short-lived cloud credential by exploiting a misconfigured OpenID Connect binding in the deploy pipeline

    • → Uses the short-lived credential to pull a long-lived cloud credential

    • → Finds an SSH key with the long-lived cloud credential

  • Phase #4: Get access to customers’ AI provider keys (3 steps in 3 hours):

    • WIth cloud access, they query the production database and access encrypted environment variables. The attacker filters for AI provider keys

    • → Figures out that there’s a key management service that can decrypt the keys, which the attacker has access to with their access to the cloud environment

    • → Calls the key management service to decrypt customer secrets (AI provider keys)

Let’s visualize how the attack unfolded:

I talked with Railway founder and CEO Jake Cooper, who said the attack was especially frustrating because at one point, they were only minutes behind the attacker: it was down to 1-8 minutes that the attack could unfold in the way it did because Railway’s team was alerted to their build system’s credentials being probed on internal systems eight minutes after the attacker started in phase #2. Railway revoked credentials the attacker used to download the monorepo just one minute after the attacker used them:

What makes attacks by abliterated AI models different

Railway’s summary is the first in-depth account of how an attack from an offensive AI model plays out, and there are several noteworthy details:

From the attacker’s side:

  • Stolen code can be exploited within hours by an AI model. If a human got access to Railway’s monorepo, it would have likely taken days or weeks for them to figure out the weaknesses to launch further attacks at. But with AI models, all this is sped up: six hours after downloading the code, the attacker figured out a plan to get access to the AI provider keys, and knew where to look from then on.

  • Abliterated AI models are like bloodhounds: relentless in chasing their goal. The offensive AI model just kept going and going, trying to get access to ever more systems with the sole goal of accessing AI provider keys. It’s hard to imagine such durability by a human in keeping going through hoop after hoop to finally get access to AI keys!

  • Attackers never give up, not even after all doors and windows are sealed shut. Railway evicted the attacker and revoked all the paths they used to get in. But the attacker returned and probed for new weaknesses the same night!

From the defender’s point of view:

  • Storing hashes of customer secrets is a very smart approach. As soon as Railway discovered the breach, they sent over the hashes of AI provider keys to all AI providers, so those providers could cancel them to avoid the attacker draining customer accounts. Hashing allowed Railway to send the keys without knowing them, and for providers to revoke them immediately.

  • Defenders are handicapped by models’ capabilities. Attackers have access to abliterated AI models, while the models Railway has for defense – from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic – refuse to engage in cybersecurity activity, including defensive work. Railway had no access to Project Glasswing during the incident, which would have allowed removal of some restrictions. As of today, Railway does have access, but many infra companies don’t have that privilege.

  • Railway decided to move to a new build system, instead of patching the existing one. Once Railway realized that its build infra was how the attacker gained entry, they shut down all builds. This was a problem for customers, given they needed to re-deploy builds with rotated keys! Railway decided to move every customer to an unreleased build system, and not attempt to patch the existing one. Fortunately for Railway, they had the new build system nearly ready to go!

During such an attack, the vendor often has to very quickly choose between “bad” and “worse” decisions. Railway faced a couple of these:

  • To simply notify customers that their API keys were leaked, or immediately notify vendors like Anthropic and OpenAI, sending over API key hashes? Railway did the latter at the risk of upsetting some customers, and even causing unaffected customers’ services to stop working until they created and set up a new API key. The trade-off was that this limited overall financial damage.

  • Should Railway have allowed builds to happen after revoking the attacker’s build system credentials? Allowing customers to do builds would have meant less service disruption, but the attacker could have returned via a slightly different path and stolen the rotated keys. Railway decided to bite the bullet by halting builds and rebuilding its build system in a matter of hours.

Lessons from this incident

I’m impressed by how much Railway has reflected on the structural problems that made it easier for the attacker to succeed, and how the company fixed them:

  • Builds should not run on shared machines. The whole attack started with the attacker being able to attack the build’s isolation boundary (the sandbox on the VM), and getting access to the build machine’s environment. Since that build machine ran several customers’ builds, it had credentials that were valuable to the attacker. Railway has now rebuilt its build stack so that each build gets its own throwaway virtual machine – which is a much stronger boundary than a sandbox on a VM.

  • Add fine-grained access control for all internal secrets. Assume that an attacker will appear within your trust boundary and try to use secrets to get access to internal services. After the attack, Railway rebuilt its CI system to separate out sensitive components, with fine-grained access control. Getting access to important and sensitive credentials now requires 2FA, and even biometrics.

  • Assume that attackers have full access to your source code. The attacker was able to come up with a better plan of attack only after getting access to Railway’s source code. Securing all of your source code is very hard – and might not even be possible in the context of social engineering attacks via an employee. So, design security as if attackers already have full source code access.

  • Decommission old, unused systems. The attacker probed credentials on Railway’s old systems, and although they didn’t get far, they could have found more weaknesses. Following this attack, Railway has shut down old, unused systems.

  • Increase logging and alerting. Even if you do all of the above, an attacker could get access to your systems in unexpected or novel ways. As and when this happens, ensure that you will be alerted for unusual usage patterns, like some services being accessed with invalid or old credentials, unusual internal network activity, etc.

  • It’s essential to respond to suspicious activity within minutes, not hours or days later. Attackers with AI are much faster at hopping between systems than we’ve been used to seeing. Defenders have the advantage that they can spot unusual patterns; after all, an attacker is fumbling around inside an unfamiliar system. But you need to act fast to evict an attacker inside your system!

Seeking to gain from competitors’ problems: what goes around, comes around

There’s an unwritten rule among software vendors that you don’t turn competitors’ outages into a sales pitch to try and poach their customers for yourself.

But Northflank evidently didn’t get this memo. On the day of Railway’s outage, the market rival published a blog post titled “How to migrate off Railway.” The article started by linking to Railway’s security incident disclosure, and explained how to safely migrate to Northflank. In the article, Northflank also boasted about its security capabilities:

“Security controls also include BYOC, workload isolation, network security, and envelope encryption, helping teams manage infrastructure access and reduce exposure.”

The article reads like a naked attempt to grab customers from Northflank’s rival, stating: “Railway got hacked, come on over to Northflank, which is a platform that cares about security.”

Any engineering teams that decided to take the offer ended up getting hacked not once, but twice. Nine days after Railway’s hack, Northflank got hacked in a near-identical way. From Northflank’s incident summary:

“The first known decryption of [customer AI] secrets occurred between 02:39 UTC and 03:08 UTC on 30 October. Northflank received its first security platform alert at 11:43 UTC, and our engineers responded within minutes. The exploit was patched within 60 minutes of notification, and customers were notified within two hours.

Some customers have reported unauthorised use of AI secrets. Please rotate all secrets now, both integration secrets and project secrets, even if you haven’t seen suspicious activity. We recommend starting with AI provider keys, cloud provider credentials, payment provider keys, private keys, and database and other service credentials.

We also recommend reviewing your provider logs for unusual activity. If you have seen unexpected AI usage or spend, contact your AI providers directly, such as OpenAI and Anthropic.”

So, Northflank took nine hours to detect that customer secrets had been stolen, 11 hours to notify customers, and – unlike Railway – they did not proactively notify AI providers to revoke the keys. Objectively, this is a worse response than Railway’s, yet it was Northflank that tried to capitalize on the security outage.

In this particular context, companies would do better to help other players in the market, rather than dunk on their competitors, and indeed, Railway’s CEO texted Northflank to offer support and information about their attack. At first glance, this might appear a bit counter-intuitive to help rivals, but Jake Cooper realized what Northflank’s leadership seems to have missed: that it’s bad for all infra providers if many of them get hacked because customers will stop trusting all infra providers! It’s in the interest of providers to collaborate on this matter and harden their own security. Once they do so, then companies win the market based on features, pricing, and innovation.

Plus, it’s just a very short-sighted way of doing business to try to capitalize on novel security incidents, especially as Northflank seems to have been worse at dealing with the breach than the competitor they went after!

I have no affiliation with Railway or Northflank and struggle to see why Northflank did not remove the article about Railway’s security incident article. One guess would be that it’s a sign the business isn’t exactly thriving, and that they’re ready to try anything to keep things afloat.

2. Native mobile & frontend jobs are disappearing

Fresh data from TrueUp – a platform that scans every open job at Big Tech companies and top startups – shows a massive fall in native mobile and frontend positions, while forward-deployed engineering demand has exploded. This finding comes from fellow Substack writer and product manager, Lenny Rachitsky, in his recent tech jobs deepdive:

In April, we covered the engineering job market and found the same trend of native mobile and frontend positions trending downward and FDE roles headed in the opposite direction:

The big difference is that my data showed the percentage of engineers employed as native mobile or frontend engineers, while Lenny’s data shows the drop in jobs posted with those specializations. Either way, it seems like the writing is on the wall: demand for native iOS, Android, and frontend-only roles is collapsing. It’s likely that folks in these positions are very experienced engineers, and this is a wakeup call to expand their domain expertise and become more full-stack in development work they’re willing and able to do.

Another curious stat: tech recruiter job adverts are at an all-time high – surpassing even 2022 levels:

My personal theory is that recruiter hiring is up so much because nobody can find each other in this weird job market: tech companies are overloaded with low-quality inbound applications, fake applicants pretending to be something they are not, and AI-tailored resumes that just mirror the job advert. Meanwhile, strong engineers struggle to hear back about applications for which they’d be a perfect fit.

Anecdotally, I hear many companies are hiring engineers via referrals or in-house recruiters. For example, I asked Linear cofounder and CTO Tuomas Artman how they make most of their hires: inbound applications have been the minority in Europe, but are more common in the US. Still, the vast majority of engineering hires have come from referrals and outreach by founders and recruiters at Linear. The numbers:

  • US: 39% hired from inbound applications (16 engineers of 41 based in the US)

  • Europe: 20% from inbound (4 among 20 engineers based in Europe)

So, while the spike in hiring by tech recruiters could be a sign that companies are preparing to hire more, my take is that recruitment has simply gotten harder and companies are spending more to hire the right people.

3. How an extremely efficient engineering team works: Superlogical

Mitchell Hashimoto – the cofounder of HashiCorp and creator of Ghostty – is back in the startup game. He has cofounded a startup called ‘Superlogical,’ whose team is building a new type of terminal called ‘Rex,’ which is a ‘durable terminal’ with a server-side component. Basically, your sessions don’t get lost when you close the terminal, and it does all this without a central server. I’m playing around with Rex and find it interesting.

Superlogical is only a few months old and its team members are experienced engineers who care about software craft and are open-minded about using AI as an efficiency tool. Mitchell wrote about how their team works (emphasis mine:)

“First, everyone is trusted to push to main. We do machine-aided code review pre-push and human plus more machine-aided code review post-push. Limited to no PRs.

Second, everyone can cut a release. Our release process is fully automated and when you start a release (for any platform) it triggers a Slack notification and a 15 minute countdown.

The 15 minute warning is a final gate that allows people to review plus collaborate on a changelog. During that 15 minutes, anyone in the company can pause the release rollout. After 15 minutes, the train leaves the station. You can’t override the 15 minutes (except to pause). It gives everyone a chance to step in.

Third, we avoid synchronization through fast remediation rather than through planning. The server and clients on various platforms ship features as fast as they can. We use post-hoc human review and AI-assistance to identify feature mismatches across products (”Windows has support for X and Mac doesn’t.” or “Mac and Windows differ in their behaviors for Y in this way.”).

This avoids expensive “sync” meetings and coordination. We trust that producers of features are mindful of what they’re producing, and we trust that adjacent product lines will self-synchronize quickly. In practice, we see feature parity across platforms within 24 to 48 hours.

All of this works on mutual trust. It ONLY works with mutual trust.

But this is already a markedly different practice than what I would’ve done 15 years ago.”

The interesting thing is that so much of this company’s working style rests on trust: colleagues trust each other to move fast without code reviews or pull requests, and leave it up to individual engineers to decide when to do them. Sure, the team uses AI assistance, but their working style is not about AI, but working as a team.

Mitchell describes this working style in more detail in a detailed post.

4. Industry pulse

Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of NVIDIA

Today, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of NVIDIA, in a swift downfall brought about by allegations he had an affair with a Chinese spy. It’s a big event because NVIDIA is built so much around Jensen; his obsession with detail and winning, and an extremely flat management structure. Jensen resigned a week after allegations surfaced. Here’s how events played out:

  • 6 Nov: The New York Times and Financial Times reported that Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, an AI cloud and data center company in Singapore.

  • 8 Nov: Jensen Huang admits he was unfaithful to his wife and apologizes to her and the company

  • 11 Nov: The New York Times reports a second, romantic relationship with a subordinate at NVIDIA that Jensen had

  • 12 Nov (today): Jensen Huang resigns.

Of course, there’s politics involved: the US had been investigating Megaspeed since October 2025 for allegedly circumventing controls by selling GPUs in China in breach of US export rules. US officials recently confirmed that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy, and the story snowballed from there.

The high-flying executive had little option but to step down given all that context, and his departure is a massive loss for NVIDIA.

OpenAI buys Pierre Computer

There have been three notable startups gunning to build the “GitHub for the AI age:” Entire (cofounded by GitHub’s last CEO, Thomas Dohmke), Cursor Origin (built by the Graphite team, acquired by Cursor, then Cursor acquired by SpaceX) and the Pierre Computer Company.

Last week, OpenAI announced it has acquired Pierre Computer Co. From the sound of it, OpenAI will integrate Pierre’s version control into Codex, and I can see them making code storage available as an additional service in the future. OpenAI itself confirms this is the goal:

“Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.”

Carta sells a coding harness

Carta is the leading equity management platform in the US, and despite not being a dev tools company, the fintech has launched a collaborative coding harness, Evergreen:

Carta built this system for itself in July of this year, and saw a major increase in PR output because of the collaboration. Then, they decided to make it into a product and completed the work of “externalizing” it in only a month or two, at my estimation. Pricing is usage-based: charging per millions of tokens used, on top of the provider’s price.

Carta is the second major fintech to launch a collaborative coding harness as a standalone product, after Ramp did so with Inspect.

One obvious impact of AI is that a lot of non-devtools companies are launching devtools products, because it’s much easier to build and ship such products!

Meta buys Conductor & closes it

Conductor is – or was – an AI dev tool for running and managing multiple coding agents in parallel – like using Claude Code and Codex agents all at the same time. Conductor raised a $22M Series A round back in March, which looked like an indicator that the company was here to stay.

But it’s not, as Meta has other ideas. The social media giant acquired the company and team, and the product is to shut down pretty much immediately. New signups had been disabled since the announcement, Conductor Cloud is becoming read-only tomorrow (Friday, 13 November), and the local service will be shut down next year. Employees will join Meta’s AI team, making this purchase an acquihire where Meta only wants the team and not the product.

The largest competitor of Conductor is T3Code – a similar solution built by the software engineer and YouTuber, Theo Browne. On Tuesday, at a dev meetup in London, software engineer Jorge Cohen – formerly on the React team at Meta – could be heard enthusing about how amazing T3Code is, especially for coding from his new iPhone Duo. Jorge showed me his workflow, and how he’s found T3Code to be much more efficient than both Claude Code and Codex. It’s also possible to use Anthropic and OpenAI subscriptions with it.

I suspect Conductor has been popular with devs and was an attractive business prospect. Meta must have offered an eye-watering amount of money that was impossible to resist.

World’s largest hack: Binance loses $6B

On 29 October, Binance was hacked and $6.3 billion of crypto was stolen from the company’s hot wallets. Based on the incident update from Binance, here’s how the hack unfolded:

  • June: identifying a Binance engineer. Engineer ‘A’ on Binance’s Wallet team installed a Homebrew installer while searching for an AI coding tool. Binance’s security team caught that the package manager was malicious, removed it, and rotated security keys. But the attackers had gained details of Binance’s wallet infra, and details of who works on this team.

  • Sep: fake job interview. Engineer ‘B’ was also on the Wallet team (a detail collected in June) and was invited to a “fake” job interview: an interview loop set up by the attacker. At the end of a challenging series of interviews, Engineer B was asked to download a code assignment. Running that code repo triggered malicious code, unbeknownst to Engineer B.

  • 20 Oct: machine takeover. The attackers had access to Engineer B’s machine and silently took over two more engineers’ machines. One of those machines held a token with deployment permissions.

  • 29 Oct: ready to attack. The attackers deployed a container on one of the engineers’ machines, and got unauthorized access to the internal wallet signing service, meaning they were able to withdraw crypto from Binance’s hot wallets.

  • $6.3B stolen. With the setup in place, attackers moved out over $6B worth of crypto. These transactions are not reversible, so that was that.

Attackers were able to move out billions of dollars so quickly and effortlessly thanks to a 2025 improvement in the Ethereum protocol, called EIP-7702. Before it, every transaction needed to be signed one by one – and doing so would have increased the chance of Binance spotting malicious transactions and halting them. But EIP-7702 allows transaction bundling, and that’s what the attacker did by moving $2.5B of funds in a single, irreversible, bundled transaction.

Binance claims to have frozen around $2.8B of the funds transferred out, but even so, the event is the single biggest criminal heist – digital or physical – in history.

Cryptocurrency is one of the biggest of all targets for attackers due to the potential for such massive payouts as this, and the irreversible nature of transactions. If you own crypto, my advice would be to consider how much riskier holding these assets is nowadays, and to look into more security precautions than are currently in place.

Top Types of Hidden Coupling and How to Deal With Them

ByteByteGo
Nov 12
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

When you create an architecture diagram, you usually try to show the services, databases, queues, and the connections between these different components. With the help of these diagrams, developers can understand how a request goes through the system and how the data flows. We also get to know which components depend on other components.

However, these diagrams cannot show all the things that a component might depend on. For example, let’s say you have two services with separate code and API endpoints. At first glance, you might think that these services are independent. But imagine that whenever you change one service, you need to make a change to the other service as well. Or maybe both of these services talk to the same database whose capacity can be consumed by either service. Perhaps both of them rely on a common logging system.

You can think of these dependencies as hidden forms of coupling. If not handled properly, hidden coupling can have a big impact on the health of your system. Also, it can affect how you change things in your system, or how deployments are done. Or how recovery happens. In this article, we’ll look at the various forms of hidden coupling and how you can deal with them. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The various dimensions of coupling

  • Temporal coupling

  • Semantic coupling

  • Deployment coupling

  • Shared schemas and libraries

  • Observability coupling

  • Shared incidents

The Roundup covers insights and trends from the world of software development.

Today, we’ll cover the following topics:

  • More and more Agents are writing the 1st draft of most new code. According to GitHub, more than 40% of PRs in September have originated with an agent doing the work.

  • Anthropic has gone as far as replacing Git to keep up with a constant stream of changes.

  • Anthropic’s S1 filing gives an inside look at the real worth of AI coding.

  • Beyond AI, the very foundation of the World Wide Web has had a pretty rough time when it comes to security. PHP had to ship emergency fixes for two critical remote-code-execution bugs that attackers were already exploiting.

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

1 - Agents now open 40% of PRs. The bottleneck in software development is shifting

Git was designed in 2005 for the Linux kernel. At that time, you had 1000s of human developers. Each of them committed code a few times a day. Patches were swapped over email. For a couple of decades, these things were the normal way of doing stuff because writing code was a slow exercise.

This month, two data points have turned up that show that these norms are changing. GitHub’s Octoverse 2026 reports that more than 40% of pull requests in September started as a first draft using agents. This is up from 17% in March. For perspective, this comes to around 110 million PRs in a single month that have been started by agents.

Also, Anthropic recently released an article talking about how they replaced Git in its monorepo with an in-house system known as Scion. Daily merges in Scion grew from about 2500 in May to more than 30000 in September. A team of 7 developers moved the whole monorepo off Git in five months. The team says that the new setup uses 200X less CPU and memory than the Git mirror fleet it replaced.

Of course, there are still some questions that numbers might not answer adequately.

First, who is reviewing 110 million PRs a month? Octoverse says 90% of agent-involved PRs were merged within 2 weeks. You can think of faster merging as a sign of better code. But it could also mean that reviews are not good enough.

Second, how is GitHub even able to find out if something has been started by an agent? You can also have agents that commit stuff using a human’s account without any trace of their real identity. So it’s possible that the true share of agent work is even higher.

The third question is about Anthropic’s move to Scion. Of those 30000 daily merges, how many were later reverted? Throughput without a defect rate can’t give a complete picture.

My take is that building your own version control tool used to be a sign of a huge company because doing so required a ton of resources and bandwidth. For example, Google built Piper, and Meta built Sapling, for tens of thousands of engineers.

Anthropic solved that scale problem with a fraction of the people. They were able to do so because agents did all the coding. This is where the change has happened. Generating code is now the relatively cheaper part of software engineering. The scarce resources are time for human code review, CI capacity, and merge rate. I expect the next wave of developer tooling to be about verifying code and not writing it because that’s where the bottleneck is shifting.

Build AI agents that work in production on day one (Sponsored)

Getting an agent to work in a perfect demo environment is easy. Keeping it working in the messy real world is where things get… interesting.

Get a live technical demo of Redis Iris, the unified, real-time context engine. This free session explores six capabilities that keep your agents resilient at scale.What you’ll learn:

  • Give agents relevant context and memory

  • Route requests by intent with reusable playbooks

  • Set up a single context entry point

  • Govern what agents remember and forget

  • Trace failures to their source with less custom glue

Come build agents with the context, memory, and messaging they need to stay accurate, accountable, and efficient in prod at scale.

Join live November 12 at 9 AM PT.

Register now →

2 - GitHub Universe: Copilot now picks the model, and Enterprise moves to pay-per-use

Until now, using an AI coding tool meant you had to choose a model. For example, you might select Claude for one task, GPT for another, and Gemini for something else. With the greater adoption of a model router, you can get rid of this choice. The router looks at a task and decides which model (or which mix of models) should handle each step.

At GitHub Universe, GitHub made its router, Copilot Fusion, generally available. GitHub says that Fusion Max scored within two points of Claude Opus 5.5 Max on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, at about half the cost and 40% less time per task. GitHub also shipped Copilot projects, which run agents across multiple repos in parallel.

Cloud agent sessions can now go between your phone, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. So developers can basically handle their work on any device. Also, GitHub Enterprise customers can use every Copilot feature without any separate subscription. They only need to pay for the AI credits that they consume.

Now, this development opens some interesting thoughts. Earlier, the choice of the model was with the developer. But now it’s decided by another process.

Can you now see which model handled which part of your code? Many teams have rules about where code is allowed to go. But that might be decided by a router silently.

In my view, this is pretty similar to the cloud adoption story repeating itself from years ago. For example, AWS moved organizations from owning servers to simply paying for usage. With seat-based licensing, AI spend became predictable and difficult to optimize. With usage-based billing, you make it variable. But agents that might run for hours can make things quite spiky. And hence, teams need to be a lot more thoughtful in building AI workflows.

Strategically, Fusion aims to make GitHub a model-neutral layer above the labs. This turns your models into interchangeable parts that sit behind a router. In a way, this might be good for buyers, but it might also be a little uncomfortable for any AI lab that counted on their model being the default choice. It also raises the pressure on GitHub’s reliability because a platform that runs your agents has to always stay up.

3 - Anthropic’s S-1: The first audited look at the worth of AI coding

An S-1 is the document a US company has to file before it can get listed on the stock market. Unlike a funding announcement, it contains audited financials and a long list of things that might go wrong. This is quite interesting because till now, the economics of AI coding tools were mostly guesswork based on leaks. This filing helps replace some of the guesswork with real numbers.

Anthropic filed its S-1 on October 26 under the planned ticker “ANT”. Revenue for H1 2026 was $16.3B, up from $1.2B a year earlier. It has 14K+ enterprise customers, and about 250 of them are spending $10M+ a year. Also, trading could begin as soon as November. There are reports of an operating profit in Q2 and 900% net revenue retention: existing customers spent nine times more in Q3 2026 than in Q3 2025.

Recently, Anthropic also shipped reporting tools that show customers what their token spend is giving them. They also provided pooled team budgets.

There were also some important disclosures. Four models were able to reach external systems during 3rd-party security testing because a misconfiguration left access to the internet open. Anthropic also seemingly delayed pre-training a new model by more than a month to strengthen protection of its model weights.

A key question is about how much of that 9X growth per customer comes from agents running for hours, versus more people actually using the model. Also, how much of the experimental budget could be cut next year? And it’s also quite possible that the decision to launch ROI dashboards the same week as the IPO filing suggests that customers are already seeking details about what they are getting in return for their spending.

In my view, for engineering leaders, the message is that AI spend will be scrutinised pretty much the same way cloud spend was scrutinised in 2022. It’s good to start measuring outcomes now, such as cycle time, escaped defects, and review load.

Also, the disclosure about the model reaching external systems requires developers to be careful. If a well-resourced, safety-focused lab could face something like that, other companies should be more wary of their AI agent’s internet access settings.

4 - PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities

Most security advice targets your dependencies. For example, the npm packages or the WordPress plugins. But the language runtime is a dependency too. And it’s something that’s often forgotten. If you have a bug inside the PHP engine, you can’t escape its impact with framework updates or CMS updates. Every app on that server inherits the hole.

Recently, PHP shipped emergency releases for two critical bugs. They are now nicknamed “PHP2Shell”. One of these bugs corrupts request state when memory runs out. The other one lets a later request reuse state that should have been freed. Both are rated 9.2 (CVSS v4) and allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Apache mod_php is the worst case. The demonstrated attack runs before any application code is executed. Various researchers reported the presence of these bugs. In fact, details leaked on Hacker News two days before the planned disclosure. So PHP brought its release forward a day.

The problem is that the attack traffic came before the fix. Anyone who waited for the KEV listing had already been exposed for nine days.

As per estimates, around 2.6M internet-facing services were showing a PHP version in October. About 1.9M of them (73.5%) ran PHP 8.1 or older, which PHP doesn’t patch. PHP did publish minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, but it might be unrealistic to build PHP from source on a forgotten shared host? In fact, attempts to exploit also showed up on Amazon honeypots 3 days before the leak. Did someone have the details about this weakness even earlier?

The researchers may have used AI to help find the bugs. If AI can make old and deep bugs cheaper to find, the patch window is going to go down for everyone in the industry. The cost of running an end-of-life runtime goes up in a big way. In my view, the key lesson from this incident is that developers should also list their runtimes just like the dependency packages. Most dependency scanners don’t worry about the interpreter.

How GitHub Used AI to Port Copilot From TypeScript to Rust in Record Time

ByteByteGo
Nov 10
 
READ IN APP
 

NYSE President Lynn Martin discusses AI (Sponsored)

AI is moving fast, from experiments to agents that act on their own. Few people have a better view of what that shift means for business than Lynn Martin, President of NYSE Group. At the Agentic Data Summit on December 9, Lynn joins Redpanda Founder & CEO Alex Gallego for a conversation on what it takes to adopt AI where reliability is everything, how AI is showing up in the companies coming to market, and why timely, trustworthy data matters more than ever as agents start acting in real time. Tune in at 9:19 AM PT. The summit is free and virtual and runs 8:30 AM–2:00 PM PT.

Save Your Seat

GitHub recently rewrote the software engine behind multiple Copilot products. They ported the codebase from TypeScript to Rust. Almost 800K lines of code. And the great part was that all of this was done using the GitHub Copilot app itself.

This porting exercise was triggered because the existing design was eating up a lot of resources. It was also becoming difficult to embed Copilot in other applications.

However, a project of this size would have required a big team of developers and a couple of years to get done. But by using the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and AI agents, a single developer was able to finish the whole thing in a few months. In this article, we’ll look at how this porting was done and the learnings along the way. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The need for porting the Copilot runtime

  • The porting strategy

  • How the porting work started

  • The role of agent fleets

  • How the new code was reviewed

  • What were the issues

  • The performance impact

  • Cost of porting and learnings

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Need for Porting the Copilot Runtime

You can think of GitHub’s Copilot runtime as the shared software engine that takes care of AI agent behavior across multiple products. Due to this runtime, all these products can reuse the same capabilities instead of needing to maintain their own implementation.

Originally, the GitHub engineering team had built the runtime using TypeScript that ran on Node and the V8 JavaScript engine. While this supported rapid development, the runtime was tightly coupled to the command-line application’s user interface. When GitHub needed an SDK to let other applications talk to Copilot, it built that SDK on top of the existing command-line application. When you started the SDK client, you had to launch a separate background process that was made up of the command-line application and its runtime. Requests and responses moved between the consumer app and that process.

This setup became harder to justify when the runtime spread to applications that had stricter requirements for speed, memory usage, and scale. Even if you had an application written in Python, Java, or C#, it had to hold the additional Node and V8 machinery. When you started a client, you had to launch another process and prepare JavaScript for execution. Each client had to bear roughly 100 MB of memory overhead at a bare minimum. Also, processes talking to each other added a lot of overhead. Lastly, applications had to monitor two processes, and a crash in the Node process could take the session with it. These costs were a huge problem for services that hosted many clients.

Therefore, GitHub wanted a standalone runtime library that was clearly separate from the UI. Applications should be able to load that library directly into their own process.

Rust was an ideal choice for this type of requirement. It had low overhead and predictable resource usage. An early estimate showed that roughly 130K lines of production TypeScript had to be ported. But additional logic moved out of the interface layer into the runtime. Also, you had other developers adding new features. Ultimately, 430K lines of production TypeScript code moved through the migration.

How much of your week is spent answering questions? (Sponsored)

New hires, support, PMs, and your coding agents all need to know how the product works and why it works that way. Today, you’re the one pointing them in the right direction.

Unblocked works out what’s current and relevant across your code, PRs, tickets, Slack, and production data, so:

  • Everyone gets cited answers in Slack without pulling in an engineer

  • When the answer turns into a fix, a cloud agent drafts the PR

  • Your agents generate code that follows past decisions, no steering needed

See how it works

The Porting Strategy

GitHub used an incremental, in-place porting strategy.

In this strategy, you replace the runtime one piece at a time, even when the product is under active development. The development team could continue to add new features and release updates throughout the migration.

The GitHub engineering team didn’t go for a complete rewrite followed by one large switchover. This approach would have concentrated all the risk into a single release. The replacement would need to keep catching up with oncoming changes. With the smaller replacements, they were able to make each change easier to review, test, and investigate.

The process worked in a step-by-step manner. A component’s TypeScript implementation was replaced with Rust in a single pull request, which grouped the changes for review. Any TypeScript code that depended on that component called the new Rust implementation through a thin wrapper. You can think of this wrapper as a temporary bridge between two languages. The old implementation was deleted as part of the same change, so that the team had to maintain only one active version of the component. As more and more stuff moved to Rust, these temporary bridges were also removed.

As far as the tasks were concerned, the work began with small, independent helpers that already had strong test suites and didn’t manage shared state. These early changes also helped test the build setup, packaging, and communication between languages. Once they had made the approach concrete, the migration went to more interconnected parts of the system.

Throughout this process, the key aim was to maintain existing behavior and algorithms. Broader redesigns were pushed after migration. At each step, validation was performed. They had existing end-to-end tests that checked if complete workflows behaved properly as their implementation changed. If there was a test failure, the changes weren’t merged. Also, when it came to the users, the ported components reached users through incremental releases. They often appeared in a pre-release before going to a stable release.

How the Porting Work Started

GitHub started with a few small, working examples to test the waters before dealing with larger components.

The first couple of pull requests took care of the basic Rust setup. Things like build tools, automated checks, and coding instructions. They also introduced the runtime library and mechanisms for TypeScript and Rust to talk to each other.

The first main porting change moved three independent helper functions through the complete process. You can think of these early efforts as checking whether the translated code worked well. The team also tested how Rust code would be organized, built, packaged, and integrated with existing code. This gave the team practical experience with the entire process.

The rest of the work was ordered according to dependencies. For example, you had small helpers and supporting utilities come first. It was followed by components that managed state, then tools, model clients, and other integrations.

Session orchestration, which is supposed to manage much of the runtime, was left for the end. This is because larger subsystems often needed several rounds of work.

The Role of Agent Fleets

Agent fleets played a key role in dividing the migration work among multiple AI agents working at the same time. You could have a coordinating agent investigate a large component, break the work into smaller tasks, and create other agents to handle them. The Copilot app made it possible to check these sessions and switch between them. It also let them exchange messages as the work progressed.

The team got two different types of assistance from these agents. First, you had the subagents that worked within the parent session’s workspace and returned their findings to it. These subagents were good for investigating code and answering specific questions. Then, you had the child sessions that had their own Git branches and separate working copies of the repository. This lets them make changes independently. This separation helped multiple agents work on different areas of the implementation without any risk.

One example was around the session[dot].ts file that was roughly 30K lines and connected to many parts of the runtime. The coordinating agent spent an hour reading and checking before creating anything. After analyzing, it divided the work among 15 child sessions. It made the choice of models for each task. The parent talked with these sessions and tracked their progress from beginning to end. Finally, it brought the completed changes into its own branch.

Despite the advantages, running so many agents also created some limitations. When all 15 sessions tried to build and test their code at the same time, they overwhelmed the developer’s laptop. The workflow was adjusted so that child agents avoided expensive builds and tests. All that work was left for the parent. A separate chat session took care of build access for each of the porting sessions. It only allowed one build at a time.

Much of the agent fleet’s activities involved reading code, checking for dependencies, testing, and reviewing results. Their role wasn’t limited to writing Rust code. They also helped understand the existing system and check whether the replacement kept the same behavior. During all of this, human oversight remained critical.

How the New Code was Reviewed

Developers were constantly changing the repository, and hence, code review had to check both the translation and whether the port had the latest changes. The team used a reusable instruction called “rust-rebase-review” to handle this process.

First, the main agent pushed its work to the latest main branch and resolved any conflicts. After this, it checked that any newly incoming TypeScript changes had also been ported into Rust. Deleting the old TypeScript helped bring such changes to attention. If another developer modified a deleted file, Hit would flag a conflict that had to be handled.

Next, you had multiple review agents using different AI models compare the old TypeScript with the new Rust code line by line. Their main job was to identify changes in behavior or compatibility. They also checked whether the Rust implementation was efficient enough. Also, whether obsolete TypeScript and temporary wrappers had been removed. They also had to ensure that existing end-to-end tests remained unchanged because they were the only reference for expected behavior.

The code review was done in a repeated cycle. When agents found any issues, the coordinating agent checked the findings and fixed any valid problems. This continued until the reviews became clean. Every round of fixes could be committed and pushed so automated checks could be done along with further reviews. Copilot Code Review and additional review bots also checked every commit and left feedback on the pull request.

Human reviewers focused on architecture, interface contracts, and risk factors that might have been highlighted by agents or tests.

What Were the Issues

The porting exercise caused some regressions as well. You can think of these regressions as behavior that had worked earlier but stopped working as expected after the rewrite. The team found and fixed a bunch of regressions.

A common problem was that translated code changed the existing behaviour in a subtle manner. For example, some whole-number values were changed to decimal numbers, causing issues with certain SDKs. Other differences were around empty strings, time zones, or replacement libraries that had a different way of handling errors. The code could compile successfully. But the results could not be handled by other parts of the system.

Another major group of issues was around state management and coordination of operations. For example, when an operation was cancelled, it didn’t always stop all the related work. Also, when resources were released too early, the session got stuck. There was also a loss of some features. And some of them were only partially migrated.

There were also general integration and performance problems. For example, the Rust code sometimes performed lengthy work on Node’s main thread. This froze the interface. On Windows, missing process-launch settings made unwanted console windows appear.

The Performance Impact of Porting

The rewrite brought down the overhead of running Copilot’s agent runtime. Especially in terms of time and memory. With the use of Rust, there was no need to initialize Node and V8. Also, no need to load and prepare the JavaScript application. Applications could load the Rust runtime directly into their own process. This avoided the cost of talking with a separate runtime process.

GitHub saw performance gains during their detailed testing. For example, in a particular trial, creating a client, completing a single turn, and cleaning up took 5.25 seconds before the porting and 292 milliseconds after porting. This was an improvement of almost 18 times.

They also had capacity gains. In a test where many sessions shared one client, throughput went up from 7.55 completed session lifecycles per second to 120. Memory consumption also went down. In a 10-client test, the peak increase in private memory went down from 1383 MB to 126 MB.

The rewrite largely preserved the original algorithms. More improvements could happen if parts of the runtime are redesigned around Rust’s approach to memory ownership and concurrency.

Cost of Porting and Learnings

The entire porting work cost around $120K in AI token costs. They covered roughly 136 billion tokens. Most of this volume was made up of cached input, which brought down the cost of repeatedly processing existing context.

More than that, you also had developer time that was spent on this work. Apart from the main developer, other developers also made contributions to integrations, packaging, build improvements, and reviews.

There were a lot of learnings along the way.

For one, it was critical to give clear instructions to the AI tools. Some of the initial requests to port a component sometimes led agents to translate only the central logic. The surrounding work stayed in TypeScript. The instructions had to be made more effective to handle this.

Another learning was that to perform such a migration successfully, you need strong end-to-end tests. These tests should check if complete workflows retained their original behavior. The team improved its test coverage beforehand. But additional coverage could have prevented some more regressions.

The tests also needed protection. For example, you don’t want an agent changing an implementation to make the test weaker or alter an expected result. So, you need to have some sort of oversight.

One more learning was that for such migrations, you should try to translate things first without worrying about redesigning. It’s more important to keep existing behavior and algorithms intact. If you attempt to combine the porting with other improvements, it only increases issues, time, and token costs.

References:

  • Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot
