👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

Software correctness & supply chain security, with Sean Allen

A deep conversation on the biggest challenges of developing with AI – while trying not to mention the phrase “AI” once. Why? To dig up the fundamentals that are as important as ever

Gergely Orosz
Nov 10
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Before we start, I’d like to share some exciting news: The Pragmatic Summit is returning! It’s a one-day event on 10 February in San Francisco, almost exactly one year after the first Summit. I’ll be hosting and the first few speakers are confirmed. Some faces may be familiar to regular readers and listeners!

My goal with the Summit is to make it the single best event for connecting with like-minded engineering leaders and engineers, and curious, driven people. Feedback from last year was that it was the attendees and the quality of debate that made it a standout event. We aim to deliver the same this time with the organizing team, including space for roundtable discussions, and talking with speakers who can stay around after their talk. The Pragmatic Engineer team shall be there too.

Applications are open: this summit is for senior+ engineers and engineering leaders who are shaping how modern engineering teams build software, ship products, and scale up to meet challenging demand curves. Tickets are priced at $1,000. You can check out last year’s talks, or watch a one-minute video summary.

This year’s Summit is made possible by friends at WorkOS, which is helping organize the event and is the exclusive sponsor. Thank you!

I hope to see many of you there! Now, onto today’s article.

Sean Allen is a software engineer with deep expertise in building large distributed systems, stream processing, and confidential computing. He is a core contributor to the programming language Pony, which is designed for concurrency. Sean is a distinguished engineer at Antithesis.

I was keen to talk with Sean due to his work on confidential computing at Microsoft, as well as his extensive work on the Pony language, and his passion for software correctness, which he works on fulltime at Antithesis.

For this conversation, we set ourselves the challenge of discussing modern software engineering without using the phrase “AI” a single time. Read on to see if it’s possible in 2026…

In this article, the questions are posed by me in bold font, with Sean’s words in normal font.

Today we cover:

  1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness. Why languages in the Meta Language (ML) family that are built around strong type systems catch more errors during compilation time than those in the Algorithmic Language (ALGOL) family.

  2. Does anybody care about testing? For someone passionate about correctness, Sean is surprisingly anti-testing. He argues that manual testing is the worst way to ensure correctness because you want illegal states to be prohibited from being expressed in a language – even before testing.

  3. Workloads & correctness. A more robust way of testing stuff than things like unit tests, is to define “workloads” that can be executed numerous times during a test. A common workload example is The Bank Test to stress test database isolation guarantees.

  4. Is quality a “gate” or not? It’s tempting to think of quality checks as closed gates that keep out poor quality. Sean pushes back against this; he says it’s important to consider quality from the very start, and to build with validation techniques that provide feedback on correctness. He prefers this to adding CI/CD quality “gates” late in the development process.

  5. Tech debt only hurts if you have to pay it back. Stop being afraid of tech debt because you often don’t need to pay it back at all! Sean says it’s common that tech debt is disregarded during rewrites when a system has become popular.

  6. No good fix for supply chain security. Supply chain attacks – when a package gets hijacked by an attacker and malicious code is executed on a machine or service – are very hard to defend against because languages with truly robust defenses, like ‘E’, are unpopular, while popular languages assume a trustworthy ecosystem. There’s no single or simple fix, says Sean.

  7. Garbage collection is slow – but doesn’t have to be. A summary of why garbage collection is devastating for runtime performance, and how Sean built a predictably performant approach in the Pony language.

  8. Go slow to go fast. Counter-intuitive advice: spend more time designing upfront and aligning everyone, and then you’ll move fast!

You can also watch this conversation on YouTube:

An amusing detail: Sean and I discovered we share in common a first fulltime employer. We both worked at a company called ‘Sense/Net’ at the start of our careers, although they were totally separate businesses in different countries. The founders of each must’ve been fans of the foundational cyberpunk novel, ‘Neuromancer’ by William Gibson, where the ‘Sense/Net’ name comes from.

Note: Antithesis is a podcast sponsor, but this deepdive is not sponsored by them. I’ve just been thinking a lot more about software correctness in the context of AI agents producing more code than ever, thereby creating opportunities for more bugs to ship to prod than ever. I wanted to learn more about this from an engineer with extensive experience in this area.

The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. Read the full article uninterrupted, online.

Read the full article online

1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness

Gergely: How do you define ‘software correctness’?

Sean: “It’s down to whether my program does what I expect. I tend to talk about things in terms of ‘invariants,’ which is a more formal specification term. An invariant is a guarantee that my software does what’s expected of it. But here’s the problem: in lots of cases, people don’t know what they expect their software to do upfront! They know when it’s not working, but they don’t necessarily know what it means for it to be working.

‘Correct’ software does its business purpose and doesn’t wake anybody up at 2 a.m. with an outage. That is correct enough for me.”

Your personal definition of ‘beautiful code’ mirrors this.

Sean: “I was on the CoRecursive podcast when the subject of beautiful code in Ruby came up. I didn’t really know what people meant when they said ‘beautiful code’. Eventually, I came up with my own definition: beautiful code serves the purpose for which it was written and does not wake anyone up at 2 a.m.. That’s beautiful code to me!”

Early in your career, you programmed in the Ada language. What did that teach?

Sean: “When I was learning to program, I decided to pick a language and dedicate myself to it for a while. I ended up settling on Ada and C.

Ada was driven in a lot of ways by what the US defense department wanted: a language which is very deeply specified and will not let you write incorrect programs. NASA and the US Defense Department were the types who this language was aimed at. Ada still exists today, and the pitch that Ada companies make is ‘so, you like Rust, how would you like more correctness guarantees?’

One of my great regrets is I could not get programs to compile in Ada because I didn’t know much about programming back then. It was so frustrating!

Meanwhile, I could get C programs to compile, but they were segfaulting all the time! Over the years, I developed an intuition for how to do things in C so that my programs would not segfault and die. I had all these rules for writing concurrent C and C++ correctly. And even though I became really rigorous, I’m human and screwed up stuff.

C gave me almost nothing in terms of correctness. It was just a big gun that I pointed at my own foot and shot it off with, over and over again. Looking back, I understand the reason my Ada programs wouldn’t compile was that they were fundamentally memory-unsafe. And so, Ada refused to compile, given the program would have ended up with memory corruption, a crash, or a data race.”

What about languages in the ML family, like OCaml?

Sean: “When it comes to programming languages, there’s a few families:

  • ALGOL family: the foundation for imperative programming. These are block-structured languages with local variables. Languages like Python, Perl, Ruby, C, and C++ all belong here.

  • ML family: ML languages are built around strong type systems. Standard ML, OCaml, and F# belong in this family. Fun fact: Rust is the most famous ML-influenced language today. Rust’s sum types and pattern matching come from ML.

A sum type says ‘this value could be one of these things’, a bit like enumerations in Java. You combine that with pattern matching, and then with exhaustive matching. Say I have a sum type, which could be five different things. Instead of an if statement, I pattern match for which one it is. For example, here’s a sum type expressed in Rust:

Here’s the neat thing about a sum type: say you make a change to a sum type by going from five value types to six. As soon as you do it, the compiler will tell you every single place in your codebase where you’re not handling that sixth type, when combined with exhaustive matching! In other words, exhaustive matching turns every “forgot to handle the new case” bug into a compilation error. It is a gloriously wonderful experience to work with such a language.”

2. Does anybody care about testing?

You’ve written “no one cares about testing. I don’t value tests,” but it’s odd to hear this from you as someone who does care about correctness.

Sean: “I wrote that because people think of Antithesis as a testing company, and I don’t think of it that way. I think of it as a software verification and correctness company – which is very different.

Tests are things that you do to verify that things are working, for things you have no better way to verify. The worst type of testing is manual testing. You can automate it, and get more and more sophisticated with automated tests, but you are still doing something at the late stage of development. You should do as much as possible before you get to testing.

With ML languages, you can usually represent within the type system what the states are, and what the allowable transitions are. Once you have these in place, you can make sure that things can never transition to a state you don’t expect. Being able to do so is huge!

In practice, when you’re trying to work out whether your system works, you’re not thinking about the entire thing all the way down. You’re only thinking about the stuff your type system will not allow you to express. This is the idea behind “make illegal states unrepresentable.”

Playing devil’s advocate, you write the tests first in test-driven development (TDD), so that’s doing testing upfront, isn’t it?

Sean: “I love TDD. I think it’s one of the best mechanisms for writing great APIs because you’re actively looking at how you’ll work with the thing.

Also, the TDD community loves katas (little programming exercises). One of these is done in pairs: one person writes the test, and another writes the implementation which makes the test pass. The person writing the implementation is supposed to do the simplest possible thing.

When people did these katas with me, they quickly discovered that I took writing the least amount possible to pass very literally. I would hard-code answers into the implementation to make their example-based tests pass. For example, if the only test is ‘what’s 2 + 2?’, I would just return a hardcoded ‘four’.

You get to property-based testing with TDD katas pretty quickly. The kata isn’t supposed to end until the person writing the tests is happy with the implementation, so the only way to ‘beat’ somebody who’s as literal as I was, is to start randomizing the inputs. The moment you randomize inputs, you’re in the land of property-based testing because you’re generating inputs to cover more space than you’d come up with in examples.”

To be brutally honest, if I was writing the tests, I might think you were being a bit of a jerk!

Sean: “Make that a bit more profane, and that is what people said to me on a regular basis!

At one place where all the engineers did this exercise, whoever was paired with me would come out saying they were the only one who didn’t finish. But they’d also say, ‘I think I’m going to be much better at writing tests now.’

An awful lot of what was being tested with our katas were things you wouldn’t have to test with a stronger compiler. For years, I loved dynamic languages; Smalltalk is still one of my favorite languages, and I wrote a lot of Ruby, Perl, and Python. And I told myself I didn’t need the compiler’s help.

Eventually, I realized I could get by without much compiler help because I mostly worked on small systems, and I could hold everything in my head. When I started working on bigger systems at bigger companies with more people, I started to value things like being able to delete a class and have the compiler tell me every single place that breaks.”

3. Workloads and correctness

You’ve previously said that many people don’t have ‘workloads’ in their testing strategy. What are workloads?

Sean: “Most people’s examples of property-based testing are simple:

  • Reverse a list

  • → then reverse it again

  • → confirm you have the same list you started with.

However, if you want to apply property-based testing to a distributed system or database, then the workload is a combination of:

  • Inputs: created by you to drive your code

  • Validation: whatever you use to validate that the thing is working

For example, let’s take a key-value store with three operations. The workload is the combination of:

  • Inputs: the GET, PUT, and DELETE operations

  • Validation: deciding how many keys there are, what the range of keys is, and how big the key and their values can be

When reading about property-based testing, it’s easy to think that randomness is going to do the testing for you. For example, say you pick one of GET, PUT, and DELETE operations at random. By doing so, you won’t trigger many interesting places in your code because after a PUT, you’ll probably do a DELETE nearby. The odds of doing 10,000 PUTs in a row – pushing into areas where your store needs to swap to disk, garbage collect, or reshard – are tiny. Leaving all of this to chance is like walking when drunk: people don’t get very far from where they start.”

What’s a specific workload that can help with testing?

Sean: “There’s one workload commonly used for testing isolation guarantees in ACID databases, and it’s the single most important thing you want to guarantee in a database. It’s called the ‘Bank Test’:

Let’s take this setup:

  • There’s $10,000 in the system

  • You split this $10,000 between 10 accounts. Each account has $1,000.

  • The workload transfers money from one account to another inside a transaction

While running the workload which does transfers between accounts, you have another component constantly querying the total amount of money in the system. If the isolation guarantees hold, the only value it should ever see is 10,000.

If your database is good, you should never see weird failures. But if we’re talking about a distributed database and you run it in an environment where you introduce faults – like network ones between nodes or killing nodes – then all sorts of interesting bugs start popping out. Kyle Kingsbury made this famous with his Jepsen work on distributed systems safety research; it’s in the same vein as what we do at Antithesis.

A simple workload exercises a core invariant: in this case, the invariant is ‘I should never see the effects of an operation that is happening inside of another transaction.’

So, with a workload, you set the rules and let things work themselves out? And with this Bank Test, we never specify how much money to transfer or when: it just describes how transfers happen?

Sean: “Exactly. For software that’s been around for a while and has gone through rigorous testing, no bugs should pop out of something like the bank test. But bugs start popping out like crazy once you subject it to a Jepsen or Antithesis-type experience. That’s also the type of experience that happens all the time in production environments, which software engineer Lorin Hochstein does an incredible job of writing up in his incident breakdowns.”

4. Is quality not a “gate” or not?

You believe quality is not a gate. The “gate” concept rests on a belief that quality is something you hold by keeping out the bad – but this isn’t how good teams stay good. What do you mean?

Sean: “This is a big reason why I prefer talking about correctness rather than testing.

Your system should not allow bad things to happen at all. The way you write the software and the static checks that come with it should prevent incorrect software from being created in the first place.

In an ideal world, you’d write a specification in a language like TLA+ or Alloy, and somehow go straight from that to an implementation which also has all your performance characteristics. You’d know that nothing bad can happen because a model checker proved it. However, we’re nowhere near that world.

Gergely here: we did a deepdive on TLA+, Alloy, and other formal methods with Hillel Wayne on the Pragmatic Engineer podcast.

The next level is static checking with type systems: things that languages like Pony, Rust, and OCaml do. In an interesting way, Erlang does a lot of this too without a type system, through the actor model. With a static check foundation in place, testing should be for the things that static tools can’t enforce.

Keep in mind though that every programming language comes with trade-offs. Even if one had the perfect type system, it still might lack a characteristic you need, like performance!

Gergely: Let me push back on you saying that quality gates don’t matter. The ‘traditional’ development approach has a series of quality gates: code review, CI/CD, static analysis, and observability in production. Like the Swiss cheese model, each layer catches some issues. Are you saying we shouldn’t have those gates?

Sean: “Honeycomb has awesome shirts that say ‘I test in prod’. And it’s true: everybody, whether they admit it or not, is testing in prod! None of the tools we have is good enough to guarantee correctness.

Even if you do an incredible job with a Jepsen or Antithesis-type tool and come up with great inputs, there’s going to be some data that gets corrupted at some point in your production system, which your generator simply can’t generate.

The idea that there’s a gate of ‘code goes in, quality comes out’ is a lie! Hopefully, we get increasing assurance as we go along, but there’s no gate we can know that we definitely get quality from.

When it comes to low-functioning teams I’ve seen, they do one of two things:

  • Move slowly

  • Or ship quickly, but regularly need emergency releases to fix things.

Low-functioning teams think of quality as traditional CI/CD built around pull requests, or a staging environment where tests run before code goes out to prod.

Contrast that with how high-functioning teams work:

  • Move quickly and with confidence

  • Their systems hold up without alerts going off all the time

  • They think about quality from the very start

For example, when a high-functioning team is building a distributed database, they use something like TLA+ to ensure their consensus algorithm works. Or, they put the very first version into a Jepsen or Antithesis-type tool before ever shipping to production and ask: ‘does it behave as I expect?’

Systems are easy to fix when you first create them, and really hard to fix later. I’ve seen many places launch a new system and not do any testing until way down the line. The problem with testing late is that nobody has any idea whether it’s working – or even what ‘working’ means!

Gergely: But some things are really hard to test, like Google Search. Ask ten people what the top result for “best testing tool” is and you’ll get ten different answers, and the results change from day to day! If I had to write tests for even a small part of Search, I’d struggle to say what I expect.

Sean: “There are still invariants we can test. Things like ‘if I put something in the box and submit it, I expect to get results back.’

I did machine learning work on recommendation systems for a while, and the question ‘what should the number one ranking be?’ is a very different question from ‘is it working?’ Did I put something in the box and get something back? Whether it’s relevant or not is entirely separate.

I get it. So, when you ask ‘is it working?’, you can then ask questions like: ‘is it still working at a thousand requests a second, or with concurrent requests, or if I navigate away in the middle of a request?’

Sean: “Exactly. And you can also check things like whether the results are for the actual query. You can tag each query with a marker and check that the server didn’t get confused and give results from someone else’s query.

I’m sure everyone reading this article heard about incidents where a service started showing somebody else’s account to people. And as somebody who’s had their identity stolen three times, I really hope no system is showing my personal information to somebody else by accident!”

5. Tech debt only hurts if you have to pay it back

Ten years ago, you wrote: “you don’t always have to pay off the debt you created. Technical debt only hurts if you have to pay it back.” Do you still agree?

Sean: “Yes, 100%. I very much want to build malleable (alterable/extensible) software which can adapt to new situations. After all, the situation it was built for won’t be the same situation in one, two, or three years’ time!

Writing malleable software doesn’t necessarily mean changing the code. Often, one answer is to throw the whole thing away and start from scratch.

That post I wrote in 2015 was motivated by a company with a lot of debt stacked up around how its database was set up. They had a MySQL sharding limit that was getting harder and harder to deal with. In the end, it was completely sidestepped by throwing money at a distributed database. We paid this distributed database vendor a decent amount of money. And sure, there were weird edge cases where you didn’t get the guarantees you’d expect from a single-node MySQL system. But they were rare enough to not matter.

In a lot of cases, the business changes and a previously-built system is no longer needed. It ran for three years, and then – ‘puff!’ – it’s gone. You never had to pay off any of its debt! Also, there’s the case when you don’t find product-market fit, run out of runway, and the system – and company – are shut down!”

Gergely: “I worked at Uber on the Rides team, on a mature product that made serious money. An engineer from a newer team, Jump bikes, needed to use our shared functionality. They committed a change to our codebase, deleted a test that was failing, and shipped it. We had a standoff about it. Eventually, I understood that they were thinking short-term because they didn’t know if they’d be around the week after. And sure enough, Uber sold off that business six months later.

Sean: “Sometimes you really do pay the cost of tech debt, and usually you pay it because you’ve been successful. But often, people aren’t thinking about the most malleable way to do something quickly, so they can validate things.

You can absolutely code yourself into a corner with too much tech debt before you’ve even found product-market fit. But the idea that every single bit of debt is bad and must always be paid off is not borne out by reality.”

6. No good fix for supply chain security

Let’s talk about the timely topic of supply chain security, given so many recent security incidents. What is supply chain security?

Sean: “The easiest way to compromise a component is to find its weakest link and attack that, and this applies to hardware, too. AMD and Intel make all sorts of security guarantees with trusted computing modules, but if you really want to attack those systems, you want someone who can put malicious firmware onto the machines while the hardware is being assembled.

With software, a great way in is to go after something people use without thinking about much, like a component in a CI/CD system. If you get your code running inside a CI/CD system, you have access to all its secrets, and can start publishing software with malware in it. With almost every programming language around today, you download a package off the internet, and it can do literally anything on your machine! For example, a package that’s supposed to pad out some text is also allowed to run a crypto miner or open network connections.”

“There are a few naive defenses: you can have a cooldown period, and not take any package version until it’s at least a week old, or get rid of dependencies, or fork them. But these trade away fresh packages which often contain critical fixes for safety. What works?

Sean: “If everybody decides to do the cooldown period, who’s going to notice?

In general, for almost every programming language, there’s no good answer. Languages that might have defenses against packages going rogue, like E – which we’ll get to – are famously languages that nobody uses because this supply chain security has not been a concern for a long time.

Almost all package management dates back to how Perl has done it with CPAN (the Comprehensive Perl Archive Network) since 1995. CPAN, like almost everything on the internet, was incredibly open and trusting. It was a network which assumed everybody was a good actor.

The fundamental problem is that the code you happen to download from the internet has the exact same capabilities as the code you wrote. This is true for popular languages like JavaScript, Ruby or Rust. So, how are you going to vet all the code downloaded from the internet? People try sandboxing, but every sandbox can be escaped from – and it’s usually not even all that hard.

One area of research is object capabilities (ocap). Mark Miller was the main designer of the E programming language which has object capabilities. The basic idea is this: in order to take any action within the system, you have to be given the capability to do it.

For example, you cannot open a network connection unless you have that capability, and your own code has to hand this capability to other code it uses. However, no popular language implements the concept of object capabilities.

And even if a popular language today did, it would not be sufficient. If the language you use has a foreign function interface (FFI) for calling C, or Rust code – and you don’t control this interface completely – somebody can just go out the FFI door. None of these problems will be addressed by incrementally changing the system we currently have.

Gergely: If we do everything right, like use object capabilities and solve the foreign function interfaces, would we be safe from supply chain attacks?

Sean: “The really horrifying part is that we could do everything I’ve mentioned and more, and none of it would be a good defense! This is because years ago we made a trade-off to make CPUs faster: speculative execution. The CPU executes branches ahead of time, using cycles it would otherwise waste, and that has given us most of the speedups in the last 20+ years.

But those speculative branches have to exist in memory! Let’s say the CPU executed both the branch for ‘authorized’ and the branch for ‘not authorized’. A sufficiently knowledgeable attacker can use a side-channel attack to read the memory created for the access they don’t have. Or better yet, get the security keys out of memory.

So, we really cannot defend against CPU side-channel attacks for as long as we allow for speculative execution?

I worked in the confidential computing group at Microsoft Research, where we built a confidential container offering that’s still available there. Our security guarantees were great, but we always added one thing at the end: every single guarantee we had was violated by side-channel attacks.

When the first speculative execution attacks happened, the Linux kernel was patched for one individual case, and the first patch caused a large performance drop. Then came another attack, and another. At a certain point, people realized we’d just be playing whack-a-mole, because nobody wants to sacrifice performance. I’m very concerned about security, but in my open-source work, I absolutely take advantage of speculative execution and the branch predictor: it’s the side of me that wants to make stuff go fast and loves that.

We’ve all made that deal: we’re willing to go fast thanks to speculative execution, even though it’s fundamentally insecure.

7. Garbage collection is slow – but doesn’t have to be

You’ve said that most engineers think garbage collection is slow, and that they’re not wrong: stop-the-world collectors really do destroy tail latencies. You also said that garbage collection being slow confuses the symptom for the cause. So, what’s the cause?

Sean: “When most people think of garbage collection, they think of what the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) does. When we were building realtime data processing for banks at a previous startup, the standard JVM garbage collectors available were very disruptive: in order to collect garbage, everything had to stop; for example, a request comes in right as the garbage collector starts, and your latency goes from milliseconds to huge spikes. That’s very bad in trading systems and systems running alongside them, like a risk system that decides whether to shut down trading.

I think of garbage collection as the mechanism by which your program frees memory it no longer needs. People think of malloc and free C system calls on one side, and garbage collection on the other. But if you want to go fast, you don’t malloc and free all the time because those are slow system calls. What you do instead is allocate a whole bunch of memory at once, and slice off little bits of it using slab allocators or arena allocation. However, as a tradeoff, you have to work out when memory is free and when you can release it. By doing so, you’re already halfway to what most people think of as garbage collection!

On the JVM, all memory is basically reachable from anywhere on any thread. That makes it very hard to free memory without stopping the world. Concurrent collectors like Java’s Shenandoah collector or Azul’s, are really impressive engineering for how they manage to do it anyway.”

How does Pony avoid the performance hit of garbage collection?

Sean: “You can think of each actor as having its own heap and each is responsible for freeing the memory it used. So, instead of stopping the entire program, an actor that’s done some work checks, using a heuristic, whether it has memory it can free. It’s like: ‘I did 10 application operations, so now I’ll do one memory-freeing operation. People describe Erlang’s BEAM virtual machine in the same way.

‘What you end up with is flat latencies instead of the spiky tail latencies that are typical when running the JVM with its bursty garbage collection. The tradeoff is that with Pony’s setup, you give up a bit of throughput at your peak moment. It’s still garbage collection, just an entirely different take on it.”

8. Go slow to go fast

‘You’ve said that going slow to go fast means writing a planning document and agreeing what to do before anyone touches code, throwing away parts not understood, and stopping when production “is on fire at 2:00 AM.” But some of these seem counterintuitive to me.’

Sean: “Not to me! They were earlier in my career, though. Eventually, you realize that working 80 hours a week isn’t making you go faster: you make more mistakes because you’re tired all the time, and you spend your time tracking down bugs instead of building new functionality.

When I get tired, I should step away from the computer. That’s going slow to go fast: making sure I’m rested and healthy, and that my brain – which is a key part of all of this – is functioning correctly.

The worst time-wasters I’ve seen are people not taking the time to confirm that words mean the same thing for everyone else. Later, the thing pops out the other end and somebody says: ‘that’s not what I wanted!.’

If you’re going to build something big and complicated, it’s worth spending a few days in the first part of development not on writing code, but on writing down how the thing is going to work, and what it’s supposed to do, and making sure everybody agrees. It’s very easy to change things at that stage. Years ago, there was a wonderful argument in the distributed systems community about what ‘exactly once’ meant for delivering messages.”

Ah, exactly-once message delivery!

Sean: “Yes. One group meant exactly-once processing, talking about idempotence: a message only having an impact one time. The other group meant a message literally arriving at a computer only once, and they were saying: ‘you are liars, you can’t do exactly once!’ They spent all this time yelling at each other because nobody bothered to sit down and say: ‘this is what I mean by exactly once.’

It happens all the time. Somebody jots something down on a ticket in Linear or JIRA, you pick it up, and spend an hour, a day or five days building it. Then: ‘oh yeah, that’s not what we were expecting.’ You went fast but got nowhere.

So, spend the time to establish the foundation, and make sure everybody is pointed in the same direction. And if you want to go fast later, think from the very beginning about how you’ll know it’s working.

You can build a system where it’s almost impossible to know whether it’s working, or build one where it’s easy to know. Building one where it’s easy to know if it’s working includes the static checks we’ve discussed, and also includes good observability. How will we know if it’s down, how will we know about gray failures, where lots of people get a really bad experience, but the system is still up and responding to the load balancer?

Spend a little time upfront, get everybody on the same page, figure out what you’re going to do, and then you can go really fast.”

Takeaways

So, we managed not to mention “AI” a single time while diving into the problems AI agents create. Here are observations from it for when building software using AI:

“How can I tell if my code is correct?” is a significant question to solve with AI agents. Most of us use AI to generate code, but not so many of us always carefully read the code outputted by agents – simply because there’s much more code being generated at superhuman pace. What I appreciate about Sean is his position on tests; he’s been a believer in building and using languages that catch lots of state and logic bugs during compile time.

With a reliable language foundation in place, your testing can focus on the parts that the language does not guarantee. If you start by using a language with few to zero correctness guarantees, you’ll most likely end up with far more logic bugs, no matter how thorough your testing!

Consider “workload testing” instead of unit testing to prove software correctness. Unit tests are clearly better than nothing – but maybe not by much. It’s because they don’t exercise anything outside of rigid test cases you put together. Sean points to the well-established practice of defining workload tests to validate more complex systems, such as correctness guarantees by databases.

Clearly, setting up testing with workloads is a lot more upfront work, but in return is far more confidence in the system’s correctness than from sticking to traditional tests.

If you want to produce correct software, you cannot skip upfront planning. Spending a bunch of time to plan upfront used to be called “waterfall” pre-AI, and the whole agile movement was about avoiding big, upfront planning with rapid iterations and gathering user feedback as a result of shipping frequent software updates.

But today, an AI agent can implement a big, complex plan upfront 100x faster than was ever possible before. Suddenly, “big, upfront planning” is now feasible! This is especially true for getting everyone on the same page, and reaching an agreement and understanding about what we want to build.

With this capability, it looks likely that we’ll see the return of big, upfront design as a general best practice when done for the right reasons.

Without mentioning “AI” during our conversation, we went deep into matters that are very important with AI: correctness, validation, what quality is, whether tech debt is important, and secure coding practices. Sean spent plenty of time on those topics, pre-AI, and it’s now changing how we generate code.

Today, it’s more important to think about how we validate and secure software – ideally before we delegate to coding agents!

How LinkedIn Uses AI to Review 40,000 Pull Requests a Week

ByteByteGo
Nov 9
 
READ IN APP
 

4 Key Insights for Scaling LLM Applications (Sponsored)

The challenge of running LLM applications in production is that failures are silent, costs are unpredictable, and security vulnerabilities are hard to detect until it’s too late.

Download this Datadog eBook for practical strategies to monitor, debug, and secure your LLM application workflows end-to-end. You’ll get 4 key insights into how to overcome the challenges of deploying LLMs at scale — from tracing multi-step chain executions and detecting prompt injection attacks to tracking token costs and evaluating output quality in real time.

LinkedIn has more than 10,000 active code repositories, with tens of thousands of pull requests (PRs) being opened each week [1]. As coding agents write more of that code, the slow part of shipping software has moved from writing code to reviewing it.

To overcome the code review bottleneck, LinkedIn built its own AI reviewer. In a typical week, this in-house reviewer covers more than 40,000 PRs, and most of its reviews are posted before the first human reviewer even opens the PR [1].

To better understand the landscape of AI reviewers and how LinkedIn built theirs, we interviewed Min Chen, a Principal Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, and Balaji Srinivasan, Senior Director of Engineering at LinkedIn. Thanks to both of them for their time and for being open about what did not work.

In this article, you’ll learn:

  • What an AI code reviewer is, and why review is the bottleneck these days

  • Three main directions for teams and companies to handle the code review bottleneck

  • How to build a multi-agent AI reviewing system that works in production

  • What evaluation looks like for AI reviewers

  • What’s ahead and where the new bottlenecks move

What Is an AI Code Reviewer?

Software development has two main steps. An engineer writes a change, and other engineers review it before it merges into the main codebase.

When an engineer writes the code, the change becomes a PR. Then reviewers read its diff, that is, the lines it adds, removes, or changes. Here are the typical steps from when a writer opens a PR to when the PR is merged back into the codebase:

  1. The author opens a PR from a branch that has the change.

  2. The code host, such as GitHub, notifies the reviewers and starts continuous integration (CI), which runs tests and linters (to flag style problems and simple errors).

  3. A reviewer reads the PR and comments on specific lines.

  4. The author pushes fixes. Then the reviewer looks again.

  5. The reviewer approves, and the PR merges.

AI is changing this development process, because it can now help with some of these steps. Engineers hand those steps to AI agents and spend more of their time focusing on intent and judgement. That is AI-native development.

Specifically for the writing step, frontier coding agents have shown promise lately. Given a task, an agent implements the feature, writes the tests, then runs those tests, and iterates until they pass. Finally, it opens a PR for review.

With coding agents, writing (the first step) can now be largely automated and done much faster. Instead of an engineer spending hours or days writing a change, the agent spends minutes writing it. But if real humans still have to review the proposed changes, the process will still be slow, because engineers’ hours are still fixed and limited.

The fix is a system that can reliably review code, ideally before humans do. That system is called an AI reviewer. It reads a PR the way a human reviewer would and comments on the lines that need attention. Once the automated code review is complete, the author, in this case the coding agent, addresses them so human reviewers spend their limited time on judging the fixes.

Since models are also getting better at reading code, more teams are automating reviews this way [2]. They mostly differ in the extent to which they aim to automate the reviewing process. Full automation would let AI approve changes on its own. This is difficult, and most labs are not there yet.

Partial automation keeps human approval on changes and gives AI the first pass. This makes the process faster but keeps real humans in the loop to reduce the risk of merging buggy or insecure code. Partial automation is more feasible these days, and companies that have an AI reviewer in place, like LinkedIn, usually use partial automation. In the rest of this article, we focus on partial automation.

But why is building an AI reviewer challenging? For an AI reviewer to be reliable, it has to have four properties:

  • Grounded: it flags real problems in the changed lines.

  • High-signal: the issues it produces are real bugs and high-risk lines (not just minor style nits a linter would catch).

  • Codebase-aware: it follows the codebase’s own conventions.

  • Timely: it comments while the author can still act on it.

Getting all four at once is the hard part. LinkedIn built its own system over several iterations to get there. Let’s see how they built it.

How to Build an AI Code Reviewer

Remember from earlier that the goal is partial automation. PRs still get a human review, but the AI review comes first. As a company, you have different options to have an AI reviewer in place. Some options are easier to set up but less flexible, while others take more work to build but give you more control over the quality of the comments.

Three common directions are:

  • Use a vendor’s reviewer

  • Use an off-the-shelf model with your rules

  • Build a custom multi-agent review system

Direction 1: Use a vendor’s reviewer

A fast way to have an AI reviewer in place is to simply buy a hosted system from a vendor. The reviewer connects to the code host and comments on each new PR moving forward. So you don’t have to build the system internally.

This direction is simple to set up, does not need any particular expertise, and is probably the fastest option. But it has two major limits. First, it is generic. You can add a rule file, but the vendor controls the prompts and the harness, so many comments are generic and could apply to any project.

The second limit is control. The vendor owns the system, so it decides when the model or the instructions change. You cannot test an update before engineers see it or gradually roll out a change.

LinkedIn tried this option first. During an AI-native pilot, teams were asked to opt in to a vendor’s hosted reviewer. But the team observed that the comments were noisy and generic. They did not fit LinkedIn’s codebase and each repository’s rules. When the comments are noisy, engineers lose trust.

Soon, engineers asked to opt out, which meant the full manual review was back again. The team also had no control over the vendor’s changes. Min put it this way: “You don’t own anything. They do something, they change something, you just react to it.”

Direction 2: Use an off-the-shelf model with your rules

Since a hosted reviewer is too generic, a natural next step is to use an off-the-shelf model, but build your own harness around it. That way, you can choose your own prompts and write the codebase’s own rules into its instructions. With those instructions and more control over the harness, the comments will be more specific to your conventions.

This direction sounds promising: the comments would be specific to the codebase and would likely arrive quickly, before human review. But it has two main problems.

The first problem is hallucination. Because the system relies on a single model and there is no verification in place, if the model hallucinates, nothing will catch it. The author will end up with a comment about a problem that does not exist, or a real problem attached to the wrong line.

The second problem is knowledge gaps. A model learns what good and bad code look like from its training data. With a single model, it will work well on areas that overlap with its training data, but will fail on out-of-distribution inputs or inputs that were less frequent in the training data. That means a single reviewer model misses the same classes of issues repeatedly and may over-flag the same low-value issues.

LinkedIn also observed the same issues when the team built the review system with their repository-specific rules. The model gave good results but produced many hallucinations, and some of its comments did not even match the line numbers in the diff. Using a different model for review than for writing code did not fix the hallucination issue. But that idea led the team to ask whether a second model could check and verify the first model, the idea behind the multi-agent design.

Direction 3: Build a custom multi-agent review system

This direction relies on multiple agents to produce grounded reviews. There are different design patterns for multi-agent systems, but a popular one is the orchestrator-subagent pattern [3], where one agent hands work to several subagents and combines their results. For code review, the subagents independently review the same PR, often each with a different model, and return their findings with line numbers. The orchestrator then merges overlapping findings, ranks them by confidence, and posts only reliable reviews.

This design can mitigate most of the limitations of the previous directions because you own the whole system, different models cover each other’s knowledge gaps, and findings by different agents must be verified by others to survive and be posted.

To add your rules and codebase conventions, there are two ways. One is context injection, which means adding a rule file to the repository that the AI reviewer reads on every PR. This can work in simple codebases, but is not a flexible approach because some rules apply to every repository, some to one repository, and some to one kind of change. A single file being injected as context cannot contain all three or combine the right ones for each PR.

The other approach, which LinkedIn used, is a layered design. You design several tiers, and each has its own scope, owner, and rules. Then a dedicated subagent uses those rules to perform an independent review. LinkedIn used the following three tiers:

  • Company-wide rules apply to every repository. These can be YAML files clarifying what the model should check.

  • Repository rules cover one codebase. This can be a markdown file containing the team’s conventions like coding standards and review criteria.

  • Pull request rules apply only to one kind of change.

To better understand how this system reviews a PR, let’s go over a concrete example and see how each step handles it. Imagine an author opens a PR that has a new python file named cache.py, implementing an in-memory cache for a Python service. But the code has two problems. It has a race condition and a bare except.

The author, who may be a coding agent, writes the change and opens a PR. The PR is then handed to the AI reviewer, which reviews it in the following three steps.

Step 1: Running parallel independent reviews

The orchestrator fetches the diff and codebase context, then dispatches them to several subagents at once. A subagent builds its own prompt, reviews the full diff in the context of the codebase and its recent changes, and then returns its structured findings.

Notice that the subagents never see each other’s findings while they review. If Subagent A could read Subagent B’s findings first, it would tend to agree, but because the subagents work independently, their agreement counts as evidence.

Step 2: Merging reviews

The independent subagents from the previous step produce findings. Many of those findings may overlap, pointing to the same issue(s). For example, if three subagents find the same five issues, the author gets fifteen comments for five problems. So the orchestrator has to merge duplicates.

This can be done in two phases. First, a deterministic check marks findings with overlapping line ranges as candidates, a cheap step that limits the search to the same code. Second, an LLM decides whether each candidate pair describes the same problem. This second phase is necessary to find overlaps semantically because two models usually do not phrase an issue the same way.

The overlaps also indicate review confidence. If multiple findings merge into a single comment, the engineer is more likely to accept it, so the code reviewer can rank it higher.

The outcome of this step is a shorter list of findings, with overlapping ones merged into single high-confidence comments. However, we still need to check the findings that only one subagent raised, which is the focus of the last step.

Step 3: Verifying reviews

A finding from only one subagent is harder to judge. It might be a real issue the other model missed, but it might also be a hallucination. To find out, the orchestrator sends those to another model to verify against the code. According to LinkedIn’s post, this often saves real issues [1]. A model that missed an issue, when asked to verify another model’s finding, confirms the issue is real. Verified findings are then rated for importance.

When the verifying model contradicts the finding, its confidence score drops. Then, low-scoring findings become candidates for filtering. In addition, findings that are cosmetic, already fixed in a later commit, or against the repository’s established patterns are suppressed before posting.

With multiple agents, layered rules, and a three-step workflow, the system has all the properties we described earlier. It merges several independent reviews into one, verifies the findings, and posts the review.

How to Evaluate an AI Code Reviewer

Labs and teams owning an AI reviewer system constantly change it. They may swap models, edit prompts, or add something in the harness. To tell whether a change will make the AI reviewer better, you must run evaluations, or evals, which are repeatable tests of an AI reviewer’s quality.

In this section, we cover the two phases of running evals for an AI reviewer: before a change is released, and in production after the code merges.

Eval before a release

Before a change ships, you need to know whether the change will improve things or not. A typical process is to run the production version and the candidate on the same PRs and compare their reviews, either with an LLM judge or against a golden dataset built from human labels.

With an LLM judge, a separate model takes both reviews of the same PR as inputs, and scores them. This is cheap to run and does not need human labels. You mostly need to have a fixed rubric so the LLM follows a more predictable and reliable path to score the reviews. LinkedIn has a rubric with six weighted yes-or-no criteria, and runs every prompt, model, and harness change through this before they ship.

LLM-as-a-judge works well for comparisons [4], but it cannot reliably decide which comments are actually right. A golden dataset fills that gap with known right answers.

A typical process is to collect real PRs at the point a bug was found, and humans mark which review comments are correct. This becomes our golden dataset. We can score candidates against these labels and measure traditional metrics like precision and recall. LinkedIn has built such a dataset and is now building the eval on top of it, as a complement to its LLM-as-a-judge.

Eval in production

Pre-release evals run on a sample of PRs or a fixed dataset, so they cannot show how the reviewer performs on thousands of real PRs, or whether engineers find its comments useful. Those kinds of measurements can be obtained only from production. Evaluating an AI reviewer in production relies on two things: the right metrics and a feedback loop.

The right metrics determine how well your system is doing in production. There are often so many different metrics to track, such as time to first review, cost per review, and how engineers react to comments. But some are more insightful than others. Emoji reactions, for example, are noisy because they say little about whether a comment helped. On the other hand, acceptance rate is a good metric because it checks whether the code changed because of a comment. Balaji explained what counts as acceptance at LinkedIn: “Not someone giving thumbs up or thumbs down, but the code actually changed.”

LinkedIn evaluated their system in production and measured acceptance on thousands of AI comments. As the next figure shows, engineers accepted 63.9% of them [1]. These numbers show that engineers act on most of the AI reviewer’s comments, with the highest rates on concurrency bugs and dead code (100%) and logic errors (80%).

We talked about metrics, but the more important part of evaluation in production is to have a feedback loop: a mechanism that turns those measurements into actual fixes.

As you measure your system with different metrics, you learn where the gaps are. If you run and measure your system every day, you can close those gaps. For example, LinkedIn now runs its acceptance check daily and produces a trend report of which rules and prompts are gaining or losing acceptance. The team uses it to decide which rules to disable and which prompts to change.

That is evaluation. Pre-release evals check whether a change is safe to ship, and the daily loop measures the system in production and improves it over time.

What’s Next

In Balaji’s view, the next bottleneck after review is confidence in the quality of the software as a whole, which takes more than reviewing each PR. He does not expect review to stop being a bottleneck until automated validation is in place. Deploying, monitoring, and handling incidents also take more effort than development, so LinkedIn is aiming AI tools there too. As he put it, “the faster we are pushing out code, the faster we are potentially breaking production.”

LinkedIn’s next step for its AI reviewer is a risk heat map: an optional feature that will score each region of a PR’s diff by predicted risk so that engineers review the riskiest parts first.

References

[1] High-Signal AI Code Review That Adapts to Your Codebase at Scale: https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/high-signal-ai-code-review-that-adapts-to-your-codebase-at-scale

How I use AI

Ben Stolovitz

23 minutes by Ben Stolovitz AI tools have changed dramatically in just 12 months. Coding agents now write over 90% of the code, handling features and bug fixes while humans focus on architecture and quality. AI search, tutoring, and transcription work well, though writing assistance remains mediocre and AI art feels like a net negative when used commercially. The technology is powerful, but how we choose to use it still matters most.

Updating a vector database is no simple thing

Doug Turnbull

8 minutes by Doug Turnbull Doug explains the challenges of updating vector databases in production. He explores how HNSW handles inserts, updates, and deletes, highlighting the trade-offs between search speed and write performance. He also compares different database approaches and recommends testing with real production traffic rather than relying on simple benchmarks when choosing a vector database.

item.title: Message queues
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Message queues

Alex Ewerlöf

13 minutes by Alex Ewerlöf Message queues sit between services that produce work and services that do the work, letting each side run at its own pace. When traffic spikes, the queue absorbs the load instead of crashing the system. If a worker fails mid-task, the message is redelivered rather than lost. Choose a queue for async tasks, bursty traffic, or when reliability matters, but avoid them when you need fast, synchronous responses.
item.description: Message queues

item.title: Little things
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Little things

Paul W. Homer

6 minutes by Paul W. Homer Good coding habits matter more than most people think. Paul suggests setting up your environment and foundations before writing core logic, and always answering open questions early rather than assuming. Use lots of small, well-named functions instead of comments, keep loops minimal, and never sacrifice readability for cleverness. When something feels wrong or repetitive, stop and find a smarter approach. We replaced Redis with MySQL for inventory reservations—and it

item.title: scaled
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
scaled

Emilie Noel

11 minutes by Emilie Noel Shopify replaced Redis with MySQL for inventory reservations during checkout, using MySQL 8's SKIP LOCKED feature to handle concurrent purchases without overselling. The key design stores one row per inventory unit instead of one row per item, reducing lock contention at scale. The biggest surprise was that the real bottleneck was database connection usage from unrelated checkout code, not the reservation queries themselves. Fixing that, plus a configuration update, cut primary database reads by 50% and kept CPU well under 50% during peak traffic. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: scaled

item.title: A queue is a shock absorber, not a pump
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A queue is a shock absorber, not a pump

Irina Dominte

Queues absorb traffic spikes by storing excess work temporarily, but they cannot increase how fast work gets done. If your average load already exceeds consumer capacity, the queue just grows endlessly. Watch the trend in queue depth and message age, not just the size at one moment. When the average is too high, your only real options are adding capacity or rejecting excess work before it enters the queue.
item.description: A queue is a shock absorber, not a pump

C# 15 collection expression arguments: What's new vs C# 12 and 13

Laurent Kempé

Laurent explains the new collection expression arguments introduced in C# 15. The with(...) syntax allows developers to pass constructor or factory arguments directly inside collection expressions, making initialization cleaner and more readable. It builds on C# 12 and C# 13 features, with support for options such as capacity and comparers, while keeping some limitations for arrays, spans, and dynamic arguments.

item.title: Runtime async benchmarks: .NET 10 vs .NET 11
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Runtime async benchmarks: .NET 10 vs .NET 11

Gérald Barré

Gerald shares benchmarks comparing .NET 10 and .NET 11, showing that runtime async cuts allocations dramatically for async chains that never suspend. A 20-layer chain drops from 1,512 bytes to 72 and runs over three times faster. Chains that do suspend also improve, though shallow suspensions use slightly more memory. Async streams get about 20% faster. These are microbenchmarks on a single machine running a release candidate, so real-world results will vary.
item.description: Runtime async benchmarks: .NET 10 vs .NET 11

item.title: Spying on cursor: Agent hooks, payloads and a simple observer
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Spying on cursor: Agent hooks, payloads and a simple observer

Christophe Nasarre

Cursor exposes 21 hook points that fire when specific events occur during an AI agent session, such as submitting a prompt, calling a tool, or starting a subagent. Each hook receives a JSON payload and can return a response that blocks or modifies agent behavior. By writing a passive hook that always returns an empty response and forwards payloads to a viewer over a named pipe, you can observe what the agent does without interfering with it. The payloads can contain sensitive data, including prompts, file contents, and shell output. And the most popular article from the last issue was:

item.author: ByteByteGo <bytebytego@substack.com>

Get started

This week’s system design refresher:

  • 6 frequently used orchestration frameworks in an AI system

  • Top 6 Cost Optimization Strategies in AI Systems

  • How a SQL Query Executes Inside a Database

  • How does a request actually travel through Claude Code?

6 frequently used orchestration frameworks in an AI system

Orchestration in an AI system manages tasks across agents, handles failures, shared memory and context.

  1. LangGraph: This uses a graph-based technique where workflows are represented as nodes and edges determine the state transitions.

  2. CrewAI: A role-based abstraction technique is used here. Agents are assigned a defined role and goal that enables them to work on the tasks sequentially or via a manager agent .

  3. Microsoft Agent Framework: This framework is designed to handle organizational workflows. It also uses graphs with built-in branching, checkpoints, and human intervention pauses.

  4. OpenAI Agents SDK: An LLM driven runtime approach is used, where an agent decides whether it should delegate control to other agent or retain execution to complete the task itself.

  5. Google ADK: Hybrid control approach is used where a developer defines a strategy to run tasks and a root agent splits and distributes tasks to sub-agents.

  6. Claude Agent SDK: No separate layer for orchestration exists. It lives inside an agent which gathers context, works with tools, evaluates and keeps going until no calls left.

Top 6 Cost Optimization Strategies in AI Systems

Your AI bills can grow quickly. The diagram below shows the top 6 techniques to make your AI system less expensive.

Prompt caching: This technique caches stable prefixes like system prompts and tool schemas. This means the model can skip redundant computation on requests with a shared prefix.

Model routing: A router sends simple queries to a small model and hard requests to a frontier model. Since a lot of queries are simple in practice, this can save a lot of money.

Batch API: This technique processes large jobs asynchronously by batching the requests first and then sending them. Providers often offer discounts on batch requests.

Semantic cache: We use an embedding model to cache queries. When there is a hit, the stored answer will be reused instead of calling the model again.

Trim the context: This technique trims the conversation history. This prevents sending the whole conversation every time, which can be costly.

Smaller model: We can also use techniques like distillation or quantization to convert a large model into a smaller model.

Over to you: Which of these techniques are most useful in production?

How a SQL Query Executes Inside a Database

Parse and validate: The database parses the SQL to check it is syntactically correct and the referenced objects, columns, and data types are valid. It converts the SQL into a logical query tree.

Rewrite and Transform: The database simplifies and restructures the query tree so it can be executed efficiently.

Optimize and choose a plan: The database evaluates the most efficient way to run the query. It compares different execution plans and selects the best plan that is supposed to use the least time and resources.

Execute the plan tree: The database runs the selected plan operations, like filtering, joining, and sorting, typically from the bottom of the parse tree to the top to produce the results.

Access cache and storage: The database retrieves the required data during execution from the cache when it is available or reads from the storage when it is not.

Return rows: The final result is formatted and sent back to the client.

How does a request actually travel through Claude Code?

Most of us type a prompt and watch the magic happen. The diagram below shows what's really going on behind the curtain, based on the Claude Code source code.

Let's trace one real request: "Fix the failing test in auth.test.ts."

Step 1: The user sends a prompt to Claude Code through their interface.
Step 2: The interface (CLI, IDE, or SDK) wraps the prompt with repo and file context and hands it to the agent loop as a request.
Step 3: The agent loop plans the next move and proposes an action: Edit(auth.ts, lines 42–58).
Step 4: The permission system checks the proposed action against the rules.
Step 5: The approved action becomes a tool call: Edit(auth.ts, patch), dispatched to the matching tool.
Step 6: The tool runs in the execution environment (shell, cloud, or sandbox) as a real syscall.
Step 7: The execution returns a tool result back to the agent loop.
Step 8: The agent persists the turn to state and streams the final message to the user.

The whole system is just this loop, repeated until the model stops asking for tools.

Over to you: which step in this loop do you think is the hardest one to get right when building your own coding agent?

The Pragmatic Summit 2027

Gergely Orosz

As a paid subscriber, I wanted to share some exciting news: The Pragmatic Summit is returning. It’s a one-day event that I’ll be hosting on 10 February in San Francisco, almost exactly one year after the first Summit. The first few speakers are confirmed, and faces will be familiar to all of you keeping up with the newsletter and the podcast:

My goal with the Summit is to make it the single best event to connect with like-minded engineering leaders and engineers, and be surrounded by interesting, curious, and driven people. This is true for both speakers and attendees. Feedback from last year was that the attendee quality was what made the event a standout one. With the organizing team, we’ll aim to deliver a similar experience this year, including space for roundtable discussions and the opportunity to talk to some of the speakers (those able to stay around after their talk.) You’ll also be able to meet the rest of The Pragmatic Engineer team and me as well.

Applications are open: the summit is for senior+ engineers and engineering leaders who are shaping how modern engineering teams build software, ship product, and scale up to meet challenging demand curves.

We have space for 400 people, and last year we received 1,500 applications for these spots. When possible, I prioritize longtime, paying newsletter subscribers, and I sent this email notification first because you are one.

You can catch up with last year’s summit and talks, or watch the one-minute video summary.

This year’s Summit is made possible by friends at WorkOS, who are helping organize the event and are the exclusive sponsor.

I hope to see many of you there!

The Hidden Work Behind Every Database Request

ByteByteGo
Nov 5
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

Mostly, an application’s storage system has to do work only when users make requests to that application.

However, there’s a difference between the work requested and the work that the storage system has to perform. A storage system does extra work as well, which is equally important. It can help you find data quickly, recover data after a crash, or support concurrent transactions. But this extra work also has a cost. For example, the request might involve reading a small record, but it can require fetching many blocks of data. Or when the user requests an update to some value, it can trigger multiple writes in the storage system. Also, if you want to keep the dataset highly available, it might require much more space than the actual size of the dataset.

Read amplification, write amplification, and space amplification show the differences between logical work and physical cost. In this article, we’re going to look at these differences in detail. Here’s what we will cover:

  • What is logical work and physical work in a database

  • Read amplification

  • Write amplification

  • Space amplification

  • The amplifications with B-trees

  • The amplifications with LSM trees

  • How indexes and filters use space to avoid reads

  • How compression helps improve amplifications

  • The role of caching

  • The impact of amplification

Scaling Slack and GitHub with Maude Lemaire

Maude Lemaire shares lessons from scaling Slack and GitHub, improving performance at Cursor, and using AI while keeping engineering judgment in human hands.

Gergely Orosz
Nov 5
 
READ IN APP
 

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress; take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3

• Antithesis – use AI agents to work on critical systems without worrying about correctness. Antithesis runs your complete system in a hostile environment, analyzes its behavior, and reproduces every issue perfectly. Learn more

• Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory, and reinvented the pull request (called Trails). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out

In this episode

We get an insider’s view on this from Maude Lemaire, a principal engineer and author of ‘Refactoring at Scale: Regaining Control of Your Codebase.’ She spent nearly eight years at Slack, where she led the backend performance infrastructure team, before joining GitHub to tackle database scaling challenges. Most recently, she worked on improving performance at Cursor – including time to first token.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer, Maude and I dig into the challenges of scaling some of the world’s largest software products. We explore how Slack handled growing numbers of enterprise customers, how it evolved its approach to load testing, and the lessons Maude learned during nearly eight years of scaling Slack’s infrastructure.

She also tells us what it was like joining GitHub in 2024 when Copilot was taking off, the challenges of working with GitHub’s gigantic Rails monolith, and how Maude uses AI in her work – while keeping judgment calls and decision-making firmly in her own hands.

Takeaways from the conversation with Maude

Here are eight interesting points from our discussion:

1. Performance should matter even if there’s no competition. In 2015, the homepage of Rent the Runway took up to 10 seconds to fully load due to a high-resolution hero image on the site. Maude was told it wasn’t an issue because there were no competitors to worry about. She thought differently: “The best competition is competition with yourself, knowing that you can do better, knowing that you can drive a better experience, ” she said. Maude spent some free time on speeding up the website without asking for permission to do so because it was the right call.

2. Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid thundering herds. Here’s an example of a thundering herd: the CEO of a 100,000-member Slack channel posts “everyone gets Friday off!” In response, people start posting custom emojis – hundreds of them. The problem is that every single custom emoji has to fan out to all 100,000 users. With 10 custom emojis, that’s 1,000,000 fan-outs, with 100 it’s 10,000,000; a lot of network load! Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid this problem. In reality, the absent 24th custom emoji is not missed.

3. Event floods can cripple the machines of Slack’s power users. Event floods are the cousin of thundering herds: they occur when a single client is overwhelmed by events coming through its own WebSocket. For example, when an IT worker is logged into lots of busy channels and they all receive the “everyone gets Friday off!” message – along with all the associated custom emojis and messages. This “power user” gets a sudden influx of messages with no deduplication and they struggle.

4. Load testing 500,000 WebSocket connections the simple way would have cost $150,000 per run. A new customer with 500,000 users was about to sign up to Slack, and Maude needed to run a load test to confirm the service could handle the load. Initially, she planned to spin up headless Chrome instances – each instance running a Slack session, and that would have cost $0.37 per five-hour session, per instance. The total price would’ve been crazily expensive. Instead, Maude built a tool called Koi Pond that spins up slimmed-down versions of Slack (‘Koi’), written in Go to establish the WebSocket connections.

5. Active Record downside: too much database load! GitHub used to be a Ruby on Rails monolith, which used Active Record as a database abstraction layer. This caused unexpected load: GitHub’s home page fetched live data from the database for most reloads, and loading the home page regularly triggered 100 SQL queries across three database clusters. This revealed a downside of abstractions like Active Record to Maude: when devs used it, they didn’t know or care about the additional load they unwittingly placed on the database while fetching data for whatever they were working on.

6. GitHub could not add more than 16 database shards because of scatter query problems. A scatter query is one without a primary key (a sharding key), and it needs to be run across all shard instances. But more shards make such queries slower.

Back in the day at GitHub, lots of queries made through Active Record (many on the homepage) were scatter queries. This limitation prevented GitHub from adding more than 16 shards. I find this detail fascinating: it shows why a developer-friendly abstraction (Active Record) can actually cause severe pain at the infra level!

7. For platform work, Maude personally verifies everything she gets from an LLM. When doing foundational work, Maude pays close attention to verifying the output of LLMs because she believes that ambitious structures can only be built on stable foundations. It’s an interesting approach to separate “foundational” and “non-foundational” work in order to give more attention to the former, most critical, type.

8. Platform and product engineers should rotate more. The best platform engineers Maude has worked with are product engineers who reimplemented similar features a few times, grew frustrated with the repetitive toil, and so built tools to remove it once and for all. But an issue arises when platform engineers become detached from product development and drift away from engineers’ experience of using the product. To remedy this, Maude suggests rotation cycles where a platform engineer joins a product team to build a feature, and a product engineer joins the platform team.
