How Nvidia's New Nemotron Model Works

ByteByteGo
Nov 2
 
READ IN APP
 

Shared Integrations Shouldn’t Need Per-User Tokens (Sponsored)

Some integrations belong to the whole company: a shared Slack bot, a team analytics API key, a server-to-server credential. Asking every user to connect their own account means duplicate tokens, half-finished setups, and a new support ticket every time someone joins.

WorkOS Pipes handles OAuth and token storage so your product can connect to 300+ integrations. With Connection Sharing, an org admin connects a provider once from the drop-in Pipes Admin widget, and every active member can use it right away. The credential is stored against the organization and never sent to the browser.

See how shared integrations work →

Nemotron is a family of large language models (LLMs) by Nvidia.

The Nvidia engineering team has built Nemotron with a central design idea. This idea is to build a great language model with good capacity while bringing down the computation and memory requirements. To achieve this, they combine different types of neural-network layers. They use only some parameters per token. Lastly, they also optimize how the model generates answers.

In this article, we’ll look at how Nemotron works and the various techniques used by Nvidia while building it. Here’s what we will cover:

  • How Nemotron generates text

  • How a transformer model spends resources

  • How Nvidia’s Nemotron reduces costs

  • How Nemotron uses Mamba and MoE

  • How Nvidia trains its model

  • How Nvidia uses multi-token prediction

  • How Nvidia reduces storage for models

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

How Nemotron Generates Text

Nemotron is a transformer-based LLM. Therefore, you can expect it to work pretty much the same way as any other LLM.

In a typical LLM, you have some input text that the user sends to the model. This text is divided into tokens. These tokens can be words, parts of words, punctuation, or other text fragments. While processing, the model converts each token into a numerical representation known as an embedding. Next, you have the model process these embeddings through a sequence of layers.

At output time, the model calculates scores for the possible next tokens as part of the decoding process. The decoding step picks a token and appends it to the sequence. Then, it continues generating further tokens. For these calculations, the model makes use of its parameters or weights. The parameters it has learned during the training phase.

Nemotron’s main goal is to make this process of generating text as efficient as possible. This efficiency is critical for AI agents. This is because AI agents repeatedly read instructions, make calls to tools, get responses from those tools, and decide what to do next. You can see that a coding agent might have to make dozens of model calls while trying to solve a problem. Good efficiency can do wonders for such an agent.

Nemotron Lightning model, which has a total of 30 billion parameters, tries to optimize this repeated execution work.

How Does a Transformer Model Spend Resources

A transformer-based language model spends resources on attention and feed-forward computation.

As you already know, the model breaks text into small pieces called tokens. It then converts each token into a list of numbers. You can think of this list as a token’s representation. These numbers change as the model processes the text. It gets to know more about the token and its context. So in a way, the representation of the token changes.

Attention lets you move information between tokens. For example, let’s say you have a sentence “Adam puts the ice cream in the freezer because it was melting”. To interpret “it”, the model has to know about the “ice cream” that was used earlier in the sentence. Attention provides a way to bring that earlier information into the representation of the word “it”.

To understand how this information gathering works, you need to know about three terms: query, key, and value.

A query is the information that a user wants to know about. A key describes what a particular note might be about. A value contains the actual information that the note can provide. The model compares a query with the available keys. It then combines the values and gives more weight to stronger matches. All of these are numerical calculations.

Multiple attention heads perform several such calculations in parallel. Each head learns a different way to match and combine information. Ultimately, the feed-forward network processes the information present at each position. It applies matrix operations and executes nonlinear functions to generate another representation. For example, after attention brings the information about “ice cream” into the representation of “it”, feed-forward computation can refine that representation using patterns learned during training.

You can think of attention as collecting all the useful notes from various places. On the other hand, feed-forward works on the notes that you’ve collected during attention.

Let’s now look at the cost part.

As you might already know, a model generates an answer one token at a time. It produces a token, uses that token as part of the input for the next step, and continues. This is known as autoregressive generation. Much of the text remains the same across each of these steps. However, if you recalculate the keys and values every time, you are repeating a lot of work. The KV cache stores repeated work so that the model can reuse it. But cached work still occupies memory. In full attention, a long history means more keys and values to store. Also, more information needs to be checked at each step.

There is also a cost difference between reading the initial prompt and continuing the answer. For example, when you process a complete prompt, the model has to calculate relationships across many token positions. In a model that looks backward, the first token has one position to consider. The second token has two. The third has three. And so on. These comparisons pile up across the entire prompt.

From this, you can easily guess that if you double a prompt, you need to have four times as much attention comparison work. There is quadratic growth. With KV cache, the earlier information is already prepared, so doubling the history means doubling the attention work. This is linear growth.

How Nvidia’s Nemotron Reduces Costs

Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 model uses Mamba layers and a mixture of experts to reduce costs.

A Mamba layer maintains a compact numerical state. As tokens arrive, this state is kept updated. You can think of it like a running set of notes about what has been read. The state is made up of numerical features learned during training. You can use it to carry information across a long sequence. However, the state doesn’t grow by storing a separate key-value record for every earlier token.

During generation, a Mamba layer’s state size and per-token update cost stay fixed. You can keep updating the model without making the layer search an ever-expanding cache. With a fixed state, you also have one trade-off. Compressing a long history into a bounded representation can make it difficult to retrieve content in a precise manner.

A MoE architecture changes the feed-forward computation. In this setup, your model has many feed-forward networks called experts. A router selects a group of experts to process each token. The model might have a large amount of capacity. But only part of that capacity is used for each token.

How Nemotron Uses Mamba and MoE

Nemotron combines Mamba and attention within one network.

Mamba lets you process sequences in an efficient way. Attention gives direct access to representations associated with earlier positions. Nemotron interleaves these mechanisms so that information can pass through both as it moves through the network.

The layer sequence is defined by the architecture. Every token representation proceeds through that sequence. It encounters Mamba, attention, and expert transformations at their specific positions. Therefore, the attention layer runs on representations that earlier layers have already processed. This way, much of the sequence processing uses a compact state. Selected layers can retain attention’s ability to connect distant positions. The remaining attention layers maintain KV caches.

Mixture of experts (MoE) gives the model capacity without activating every expert. In a dense model, every token goes through the same feed-forward network as every other token at that layer. With MoE, one layer contains many alternative feed-forward networks. A router selects which set of networks is used. The selected experts process the representation. Their output are combined using routing weights.

Nvidia’s Lightning configuration talks about 128 routed experts per MoE layer. 6 experts are selected for each token. This is how a model that has roughly 30 billion parameters but use only roughly 3 billion for a particular token.

Of course, the unused experts are still part of the model. They must remain accessible for later tokens. With sparse activation, you reduce the work done per token. But the total parameter count still impacts the memory needed to host the model.

Lightning also specifies 32 query heads and only 2 key-value heads when it comes to attention. This is a classic grouped-query attention arrangement.

In a basic multi-head attention, each attention head has its own keys and values. With grouped-query attention, you can have several query heads share key-value representations. The model retains multiple ways of querying the context while it stores fewer distinct key-value representations.

How Nvidia Trains Their Models

With training, you first build a language model. Next, you teach it useful behavior. Training determines the values of its weights and the capabilities those calculations can support.

The first stage is pretraining. In this stage, you make the model learn from large quantities of text by predicting tokens and adjusting its weights to reduce prediction errors. By going through many examples, you can build representations of language, code, facts, and other patterns. Lightning’s base model is trained on crawled and synthetic material that covers code, maths, science, and general knowledge.

Nvidia’s pretraining tries to progress the model from a broad data mixture toward more emphasis on high-quality material. The greater breadth of content completes coverage. Later sampling places more weight on selected capabilities.

The next training phase is supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In this training, you teach the model using examples of desired behavior. You can include instructions, conversations, code, tool interactions, and structured responses.

In Nvidia’s SFT recipe, user and system messages provide context. But the training objective is calculated on assistant tokens. Therefore, the model learns which responses should be produced for a specific conversation. If you have a task that needs structured output, the desired response can provide an example of the correct information and the required JSON format.

Reinforcement learning adds feedback to the model’s own attempts. Lightning uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The model generates several responses to a prompt. Those responses receive rewards. The training procedure compares their relative performance to update the model.

The complete training recipe includes an environment that evaluates mathematical answers, executes code against tests, checks instruction compliance, and validates output schemas.

As you can see, there is a logical progression in the training stages. Pretraining helps develop broad predictive capabilities. SFT provides examples of useful behavior. Reinforcement learning refines behavior using feedback on generated attempts.

How Nvidia Uses Multi-Token Prediction

Even if you make each token cheaper, ordinary generation can’t proceed sequentially. The next token depends on the preceding sequence, including tokens that have just been generated.

Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains an auxiliary mechanism to predict further ahead. At inference time, these predictions can support speculative decoding. In this approach, you have a lightweight drafting mechanism that proposes several candidate tokens. The main model evaluates the proposed continuation in a verification pass.

When you accept several proposed tokens, you can have token generation advance by several positions while needing fewer sequential passes through the main model. If you reject a proposal, generation continues from the accepted prefix.

Nvidia’s models ship with integrated MTP capabilities and separate draft models.

How Nvidia Uses Low-Precision Numbers to Reduce Storage

Nvidia also made another optimization regarding how the numbers involved in the calculations are represented.

A BF16 weight uses 16 bits. If you represent the weights with fewer bits, you can reduce the storage requirements. Also, reduce the amount of data transferred through memory. The challenge is approximation error because a smaller set of numbers cannot reproduce every original weight in an exact manner.

Nvidia uses the NVFP4 format. It combines four-bit floating-point values with scaling information. Groups of 16 values share an FP8 scale, with an additional scale at the tensor level. Nvidia also uses quantization-aware distillation (QAD). In QAD, you first create a quantized student model from a BF16 model. The BF16 model remains fixed as the teacher. The student trains with simulated quantization and learns to bring its output scores closer to the teacher’s scores.

Nvidia was able to reduce the size of the model from approx. 66 GB for BF16 to approx. 22 GB for the NVFP4 checkpoint.

Conclusion

Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Super has approx. 120 billion total parameters and 12 billion active parameters. With Ultra, they have scaled this figure to 550 billion total and 55 billion active. Both models use the hybrid Mamba-attention design and introduce LatentMoE.

LatentMoE addresses another cost of expert processing.

The movement of wide token representations and loading expert weights can be quite expensive. The solution is to project the representation into a smaller space for the routed expert computation. Experts process this compact representation. Their outputs are combined, and the result is projected back to the main model dimension. If you reduce the width of the routed computation, you can save memory traffic and communication. Nvidia uses those savings to support more experts and more active expert combinations at a similar inference budget.

The Ultra model also adds a new training technique called multi-teacher on-policy distillation. The model generates its own attempts and receives guidance from multiple domain-specialized teacher models. “On-policy” means learning from attempts generated by the current student. This lets the teacher models guide situations that the student model actually encounters.

References:

  • Nemotron 3 family white paper

  • Nemotron 3 Super: Open, Efficient MoE Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Model

  • Inside Nvidia Nemotron 3: Techniques, Tools, and Data that make it efficient and accurate

item.title: What's in a task?
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
What's in a task?

Ricardo Peres

Tasks in .NET run operations in the background without blocking the main thread. You can either wait for a task to finish using await, or let it run in the background without waiting. If you skip await, you must manually check if the task completed, was cancelled, or threw an error. Ignoring these checks can cause blocked threads or missed exceptions.

item.title: Prompts are dead; long live loops.
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Prompts are dead; long live loops.

Jesse Liberty

Loop programming lets an AI agent act, check its own results, and try again until the output meets a set standard or hits a safety limit. The Microsoft Agent Framework supports this with loop wrappers and evaluators, which control when the agent stops or keeps going. A marker evaluator looks for a keyword like "DONE," while a judge evaluator asks a second model to rate the output. Always set a maximum iteration count and a timeout to prevent runaway costs.
item.description: Prompts are dead; long live loops.

item.title: How fast can you fix a UTF-16 string?
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How fast can you fix a UTF-16 string?

Daniel Lemire

C# strings can contain broken character pairs that should never be written to disk or sent over a network. New functions in the SimdUnicode library detect and fix these broken strings using the same approach already shipped in Chrome. The functions process data in parallel using special processor instructions, reaching speeds around 69 GB/s on Intel hardware. When the input is already valid, fixing it is roughly as fast as a plain memory copy.
item.description: How fast can you fix a UTF-16 string?

item.title: Primary constructors are more than syntactic sugar
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Primary constructors are more than syntactic sugar

Steven Giesel

Primary constructors and regular constructors look the same but initialize fields at different times. With a regular constructor, fields are assigned after the base constructor runs. With a primary constructor, the compiler stores parameters in hidden fields before calling the base constructor. This matters when a base constructor calls virtual members, since those members may read fields that aren't set yet in the regular case but are already ready with a primary constructor.
item.description: Primary constructors are more than syntactic sugar

item.title: How to loop through a list – benchmarked
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to loop through a list – benchmarked

Khalid Abuhakmeh

Use foreach by default to loop through a list in C#. Switch to a for loop when you need the index or want to replace items. Avoid modifying a list inside foreach as it throws an InvalidOperationException. For raw speed, CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan is about 20% faster than for or foreach, while List.ForEach and Index are slower and allocate extra memory. item.title: Why I am a programmer
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why I am a programmer

Alfie John

5 minutes by Alfie John Growing up before the internet, a kid discovers the underground world of BBSs, pirated games, and the mesmerizing digital art that played before them, called demos. Stumbling onto a tutorial series about how to create these effects sparks a deep desire to go from spectator to creator. It is a story about how exposure to something mind blowing at a young age can set the course of a life.

item.title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Getting good at AI takes time and practice

Sean Goedecke

3 minutes by Sean Goedecke It shouldn’t be surprising that working with AI involves actual skills. It’s like working with a really weird person: a savant with mad skills in some areas and huge gaps in others, a prolific but inexpert communicator, a workaholic with no long-term memory, and so on. If you were a manager and had someone like that as your employee, you could likely get a lot of value out of them, but it would take time to figure out how.

item.title: The compiler was supposed to end programming too
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The compiler was supposed to end programming too

Hatim Rih

14 minutes by Hatim Rih AI tools are changing software development fast, but not ending it. Agents now handle routine coding tasks overnight, yet they still stop when a decision requires human judgment. Adoption is high but satisfaction is mixed, and teams are drowning in code faster than they can review it. The hardest parts of the job, deciding what to build and verifying it works correctly, remain stubbornly human.
item.description: The compiler was supposed to end programming too

item.title: Backups aren't simple
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Backups aren't simple

Aleksandar Filipovski

10 minutes by Aleksandar Filipovski Data loss is more common than most people expect, and simple backups are not enough. A good backup system needs multiple copies across different storage types, with one kept offsite. It also needs point-in-time snapshots so you can recover from mistakes, not just hardware failure. Rather than building this yourself, mature tools like Borg or Restic handle the hard parts, but you must regularly test restoring your data or none of it matters.
item.description: Backups aren't simple

AI Terms You Need to Know

Agentic AI: It's an AI system that describes the behavior of the whole system. The agent understands and interprets the goal. It creates a plan and calls tools and APIs to get the results. The agent evaluates the results and corrects the mistakes. It keeps on improving the results until it achieves the desired goal.

Large Reasoning Model: It’s a type of model that is trained to solve problems which require lots of logical steps. It breaks a problem into smaller problems and performs reasoning on them to come up with the right answer.

Vector Database: It's a type of database that stores vectors, as the name implies. These vectors are actually lists of numbers which represent the meaning and characteristics of text, audio, video or other data.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): It's a technique to provide relevant information to the model when needed. The relevant information is mostly stored in a vector database, but retrieval can also be through APIs, SQL, or hybrid search.

Model Context Protocol (MCP): It provides a standard interface to AI applications to connect and access external tools and APIs. The communication happens through the MCP client within the AI applications communicating through MCP servers.

GPT-2 to GPT-6: What Actually Changed

It's been seven years from GPT-2 to GPT-6, and a lot has changed.

The diagram below shows each generation and its key highlights, based on the public information we know.

GPT-2 (2019): More like a prototype to validate the potential of the decoder-only transformer. This was a 1.5B-parameter model that only went through pre-training with next-token prediction. The trained model was only capable of continuing text, not answering questions.

GPT-3 (2020): The same recipe as GPT-2, just much bigger and trained on more data to test how far scale alone could go. GPT-3 had 175B parameters, more than 100 times the size of GPT-2, and still only went through pre-training. The scale allowed it to show in-context learning capabilities. When shown some examples, the model could follow them.

GPT-4 (2023): On top of pre-training, OpenAI fine-tuned it with RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), so it was not just a completion model but could actually answer questions. It was also multimodal, meaning that it could process input images as well as text, and it handled up to 32K tokens of context.

GPT-5 (2025): The first GPT generation with built-in reasoning. Given a prompt, tools, and an effort level, the trained model could generate reasoning tokens before the answer. Its context window grew to 400K tokens, with a router in ChatGPT to decide when a prompt needed thinking mode.

GPT-6 (2026): This new model has a bigger context window (1.05M), supports async tool calling, and is generally safer. An interesting feature, called mid-turn steering, is that it can take a new instruction while it's thinking.

Al Topics to Learn before Taking Al/ML Interviews

AI interviews often test fundamentals, not tools. This visual splits them into two buckets that show up repeatedly: Traditional AI and Modern AI.

Traditional AI focuses on fundamental ML topics, mostly from before neural networks became dominant.

Modern AI focuses on neural network foundations and newer concepts like transformers, RAG, and post-training.

Interviewers generally expect you to know both. They expect you to explain how they work, when they break, and the trade-offs.

Use this as a checklist, and make sure you can explain each topic clearly before your next AI interview.

Over to you: which topic here do you find hardest to explain under interview pressure? What else is missing?

How GPUs Work at a High Level

When people say GPUs are powerful, what they really mean is this: GPUs are built for massive parallelism from the ground up.

Let’s break down what’s happening under the hood.

At the top level, a GPU chip is made up of many Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). Think of SMs as mini parallel engines replicated across the chip. Instead of one big brain, you get dozens of smaller ones working simultaneously.

Inside each SM:

  • A Warp Scheduler decides which group of threads (a warp) runs next.

  • Dozens of CUDA Cores execute instructions in parallel.

  • A Register File stores thread-local data at ultra-low latency.

  • Load/Store units move data between registers and memory.

  • Texture units handle specialized memory operations.

  • L1 Cache provides fast, on-SM data access.

Each SM works independently, but they’re connected through an on-chip interconnect. Below that sits the L2 Cache, shared across all SMs. This is the coordination layer. If one SM misses in L1, it checks L2 before going to global memory.

Then come the Memory Controllers, which interface with Global Memory. This is where things get interesting:

  • Extremely high bandwidth

  • Much higher latency than on-chip memory

That’s why GPUs rely on massive parallelism. While some threads wait on memory, thousands of others keep executing.

  • Track AI spending: Monitor costs across teams, features, and users to identify what’s driving your bill.

  • Optimize prompts and caching: Reduce redundant model calls and avoid unnecessary token consumption.

  • Manage agent context: Keep context windows lean and prevent expensive agent loops.

  • Use smaller models: Replace costly large-model calls with smaller models where appropriate.

  • Build intelligent model routers: Route requests to the most cost-effective models while maintaining quality.

  • Control multi-agent costs: Estimate spending, catch runaway retries, and optimize agent workflows.

👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

The Pulse: Anthropic kills the coding interview

AI is rendering the Leetcode-style interview pointless and now Anthropic has deleted it from its interview loop. Also: details of incident.io’s AI spend, Microsoft’s exit offer to engineers, and more

Gergely Orosz
Oct 30
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover:

  1. Anthropic kills its coding interview. A team at the leading frontier AI company gets zero signal from DSA interviews and so has removed it from the engineering recruitment process. The rest of the company, and other AI-native startups, could follow.

  2. Details on incident.io’s AI spend and ROI. The resiliency startup has slashed the amount it spends on AI; down from $4,500 per dev, per month, in August, to $1,600 now.

  3. Amazon formally incorporates AI usage into SDE and SDM expectations. AI has been placed at the heart of software engineering after the company found a correlation between AI usage and productivity. Also, software development engineers (SDEs) and managers (SDMs) must be close to customers.

  4. Microsoft issues new exit offers to engineers. The tech giant has offered 60,000 employees the opportunity to quit by the end of the year. But the exit package is not particularly tempting, and so the number of people who take it will surely be in the thousands, not tens of thousands.

  5. Security incidents continue. Since last week, incidents have continued to be reported, and that may not change for the foreseeable future.

The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. Read the full article uninterrupted, online.

Read the full article online

1. Anthropic kills its coding interview

A hiring manager at Anthropic who has led Claude Cowork and Claude Desktop, revealed that they have stopped asking coding questions to candidates for software engineering jobs. From Felix Rieseberg’s blog post (emphasis mine):

“This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them. It had a good run: Being able to quickly define problems and find elegant solutions was a weak, but useful, predictor for how successful you’d be on my teams. Small coding challenges in real code did tell us something meaningful about candidates.

That’s no longer true. There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests.

The coding interview was, despite its ubiquity, never popular. I suspect that established engineers will still have strong reactions to its disappearance — if only for what it says about the evolution of our roles. Plenty of ink has been spilled to describe how AI is a challenge for junior developers, especially those trying to land a job. Now that I’ve seen junior people work with AI for a bit, I have a more hopeful take: impact is less bounded by how many years of accumulated knowledge in frameworks and libraries you’ve gathered.

I’m seeing engineers who are comparatively new fly past people who are probably better coders and have been around much longer. Hunger beats tenure.”

Independently, I posted observations about a silent but growing divide in the industry which also involves tenure becoming less important:

“I’m starting to sense a divide in the tech industry:

1. People thriving on autonomy who are reinventing how they work and what tools they use with AI: they do lots of work, but they’re enjoying it and getting very efficient.

2. People used to being mentored / trained / or simply told what to do, and how. Frustrated with the lack of guidance from management on what to do with AI, and also frustrated by seeing some of their peers thriving. Increasingly bitter about AI and the state of the industry as a whole.

The thing is, the current change is SO fast that anyone waiting or hoping for directions on how to use AI efficiently for work, may find it comes too late.

Team dynamics are also shifting very quickly: tenure no longer automatically correlates with doing better, faster or higher-quality work!”

The tenure issue is interesting because length of service has long been something of a prerequisite for promotion to the senior software engineer role, and it was generally expected for candidates to rack up five or more years as a fulltime engineer first. This is based on the idea that it takes repetition, practice, failures, and learning, to become good enough at coding and debugging for a promotion.

In context, Felix makes it sound like promotion by tenure will not be a thing at Anthropic:

“As a longtime hater of promotions by tenure, I can’t help but be optimistic. I’ve already seen my fair share of popular apps and products made this way [by promoting based on impact, not tenure].”

A case of tenure and impact not being very related which Felix cites is that of two relatively new engineers – Anthony Morris and Alice Zhao – who built the prototype of Claude Cowork in a single weekend, and which their team shipped eight months later. Without the two less experienced engineers, Claude Cowork might not exist, or have been created much later. They were possibly not as “good” at coding as some devs with 10+ years of experience, but they were hungry, took initiative, and used AI as a tool to build a prototype. That prototype made the case to launch a full product.

But if coding interviews vanish, what will candidates be interviewed about? Among whitecollar jobs, software engineering is one of the very few where it’s possible to spend up to half an interview doing the primary task of the job: writing code! And it’s pretty measurable.

Compare that with interviews for roles in product and engineering management, which are more subjective. The engineering manager interview loops I designed and took part in were always bespoke for the role we were hiring for, and unstandardized. Felix says he has yet to figure out a definitive new structure for interviews:

“I’m probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview people who build well with AI. I haven’t quite gotten there yet — but I’m scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I’d love to hear how.”

My hunch is that software engineering interviews will become more similar to those for product manager positions:

  • Personal record in projects built and business impact made, matters more.

  • PM interviews often contain a business case takehome, perhaps candidates for engineering roles will build prototypes that solve business problems. Their solutions could be evaluated by how well they fix a problem or edge case, as much as by their architectural features. Maybe candidates will be quizzed on why and how they built what they did.

  • The process will become far more subjective. Team members could interview candidates and get a say in hiring. “Vibes” might be important, meaning candidates are judged on how well people think they’d fit in, not just on their skills as technologists.

  • But high-level software architecture will stay in the loop, surely. It’s an area which AI is not all that great at, and even if it was, architectural decisions are as much about understanding and predicting business context and priorities, as about technology.

  • Tech discussion: discovering candidates’ depth of knowledge on how computer systems work from the code, all the way down to the GPU/NPU/CPU levels.

Software engineering interviews have become very good at measuring technical skill and implementation ability, but now most fast-moving tech companies use AI agents for implementation, the ability to write correct code is much less useful. There are similarities to how valuable it was to be able to write correct Assembly code from the 2000s. Being able to write Assembly code remains difficult, but given that compilers produce highly optimized Assembly code from higher-level programming languages, knowing how to program in a higher-order language while not knowing how to write Assembly was more valuable than vice versa.

An important caveat is that Anthropic has its choice of very strong candidates. It’s a lot easier for a leading AI lab to drop coding interviews because the most standout applicants are applying for jobs there, and their work is in public and speaks for itself. Anthropic can filter by pedigree of previous workplaces and the projects candidates worked on, alongside technical interviews that are not about coding. It’s a privileged position; most companies don’t have an inbound pipeline like that.

Still, when one of the leading companies in the industry changes its hiring process, it is noticed and gets replicated at other places. In the early 2000s, it was Google which started to interview engineers with data structures and algorithms (DSA) interviews, which then spread to nearly all VC-funded startups.

I expect something similar here and with AI-native startups experimenting with the approach. If AI coding tools keep spreading, then I wouldn’t be surprised if coding interviews are eventually dropped at more “traditional” companies as well.

For all the complaints I’ve heard about the DSA interview format for its flaws, it does have the benefit of being predictable and reasonably objective. What replaces it in some workplaces may be the opposite.

2. Details of incident.io’s AI spend

incident.io (note: I’m an investor) is a software reliability platform founded in 2021, a year before ChatGPT, that’s obsessed with measuring everything. In that spirit, the company has shared details about AI spending, changes to PR frequency, and the ROI at the company from using AI. Thank you to Lawrence Jones and the incident.io team for sharing the data!

They have come up with the concept of the “effort point” as a way to analyse AI spend. One effort point is a medium-sized pull request written by a human or generated by an agent. The measurement is far from perfect, but it is one step more granular than looking at lines of code, and lets them compare the complexity of AI-generated PRs with those written by human devs in the past. Here’s what has changed in the last two years:

Pull request stats

At a glance:

AI agents started to generate production code in June 2025, which was around the same time as the first agent-generated got pushed at incident.io. The company has used AI-assisted IDEs since the beginning, such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor.

In June this year, a few things happened in quick succession, the incident.io team told me:

  • Claude Agents launched, making it easier to coordinate several agents running at once

  • Worktree tooling improved a lot, making it easier for agents to do parallel work on the same codebase with worktrees

  • Also around this time, more engineers realized that they should be running multiple agent sessions using different worktrees, rather than driving just one session at once.

Today, nearly 80% of PRs that ship to production include code generated by an agent:

More:

  • 2.7x headcount growth in product engineering (engineers who ship to production numbered 18 in 2024, and 50 today)

  • 3.4x PR requests shipped to production in September compared to a year ago

  • 3.6x increase in PRs with no human reviewer shipped to prod (12% to 43%)

  • 4.8x increase in the size of PRs (from 22 to 111 lines)

  • 6x “effort points” shipped to prod: “effort points” awarded by an AI model estimating the complexity of a PR, and ranking it from XS to XL.

  • 80% decrease in human comments per “effort point”

  • 60% decrease in incidents per 1,000 pull requests

Stats on release frequency:

  • 47% rise in releases/eng/day when taking headcount into account: an average of 2.8 releases/day/eng, up from 1.9 releases/day/eng in 2024

  • Oct 2026: 140 releases/day to production with 50 engineers. In Oct 2024, the figures were 35 releases/day to prod with 18 engineers

AI spend

This year, spending on AI tools is on track to be around $1.6M at the company – which is a lot! We’re talking around $2,700 per engineer each month, which puts the reliability startup among the big spenders of companies mentioned in this article. Based on that, they’ve attempted to calculate a rudimentary ROI for the spend. At present, incident.io sees AI tools as mostly positive.

AI spending peaked this summer and has been decreasing since. In July, the company spent more than $300K on AI (an annual projection of $3.6M, had it continued). Here’s the allocation:

Opus 5.5 brought a massive cost reduction. Before it, the company was spending around $4,500/engineer/month, mostly on Opus 5. But now, with the 5.5 version, the cost is down to circa $1,600. Here’s the impact of Opus 5.5 on monthly spend:

Also, the adoption of Opus 5.5 has been rapid:

Cost per “effort point” also peaked over the summer. The nice thing about the “effort point” metric is that it makes it possible to compare the cost of generating a PR to how much it cost a year ago, when the company started using AI agents. Here’s the change:

Infrastructure teams spend more tokens on the same “effort point.” A fascinating detail from incident.io comes from separating the cost of an “effort point.” The infrastructure team stands out, spending ~5x more on a medium-sized PR than almost every other team:

But why the big difference? Lawrence Jones, an engineer at incident.io, explains:

“This is a great example of why it’s hard to use a single target for cost per PR that applies universally.

Our AI team, for example, does work that can be very token-intensive such as iterating on evals. Infrastructure teams might use Claude to explore production environments or do lots of analysis or run benchmarks etc which don’t lead to PRs, so their cost per-PR looks higher.

Different types of work will simply have different cost profiles.”

Measuring ROI

Today, average spend is down at ~$1,600/engineer/month, of which around 80% is on Claude, with 20% going to Cursor. The big question: has AI made engineers more productive? Unfortunately, measuring engineering productivity in only a single dimension is fraught with hazard, but a combination of insights could give a sense of where things are headed. These are imperfect measurements with their own biases, but are still interesting.

The number of PRs shipped per engineer weekly tracks with tenure. This is a very interesting finding from incident.io. Compared to two years ago:

  • The median engineer shipped ~10% more PRs (10.1 PRs in Oct 2024 with no AI; 10.7 PRs per week in Oct 2026 with AI). An eye-catchingly small change!

  • The mean engineer shipped ~30% more PRs (11.1 PRs in Oct 2024 vs 14.8 PRs in Oct 2026)

  • Tenured engineers shipped ~70% more PRs (11.1 PRs in Oct 2024 vs 19 in Oct 2026)

New engineers are told to hold off on using AI for a month after they join. The AI SRE startup collected feedback from new engineers and found that new joiners using a lot of AI right after onboarding ended up performing worse in the medium/long term.

What incident.io found is that it’s worth ignoring expectations of shipping velocity during the first month. Instead, new devs learn how to navigate the codebase. This AI-abstinent approach skews the above numbers.

Harder to quantify: shipping faster & incidents

Compared to pre-AI, how important is it for PRs to be shipped faster to production? A benefit of AI agents and AI reviews is faster feedback than waiting on someone to review a PR. Here’s how quickly the median PR makes it to production at the reliability startup:

Let’s take an average day – a Tuesday last month – when 185 changes were shipped to production, 75 of which without human review:

There are fewer incidents per change, but more overall. It would be quite the omission to not bring up reliability when talking about a reliability startup! This is both good and bad news: there’s fewer incidents per PR, but more overall due to the existence of more PRs:

The good news is that the rate of incidents is lower than expected, given the PR volume:

The team looked into why incidents occurred, and found that most outages were because of incorrect code that could have been caught in review. The team took steps to address this:

  • Improved the codebase for AI use

  • Started leaning more on Cursor’s Bugbot, added stricter rules, and saw the tool start to give better feedback and catch more code-related bugs in review

  • Newer models produced better code.

Today, most incidents are no longer due to faulty code, but because there’s information absent about the production environment. The bad news is that if this continues and PR volume grows, then the number of incidents will also rise unless the team avoids outages related to production behavior. They are working on building feedback loops where agents can observe and learn from production.

I found these data points educational, especially looking at how the “cost per medium-sized PR” does (and probably should!) vary based on the complexity of work that goes into it. Thanks a lot to the incident.io team for sharing such detailed data!

3. Amazon formally incorporates AI usage into engineering expectations

Amazon’s engineering leadership have updated the guidelines for software development engineers (SDEs) – now that AI is ingrained in the role – after collecting observations from its top SDEs. There are a few interesting details in the email to staff:

  • AI is at the center of software engineering practice. This comes from distinguished engineers at the online retail giant, who are known to have a high bar for engineering excellence.

  • “Frontier teams” are ahead: Teams that are the most AI-pilled are known as ‘frontier teams’ where productivity and delivery are up compared to other teams.

  • Teams without AI are falling behind: although outcomes are hard to measure – because projects and business impact take much longer to materialize – Amazon leadership claims that teams that are adopting AI less can be observed to be reducing worse business results versus teams that are considered “frontier.”

  • P10 and P90: Amazon is paying special attention to the “bottom 10%” of teams which are lagging behind in AI usage, and also to the top 10%. This focus is a familiar Big Tech approach.

Non-negotiable for managers to be hands-on with AI, the email says:

“As a technical or organizational leader, part of your job is making sure that your team or organization is using AI to the best effect to improve delivery for customers and your business. That requires deeply understanding these technologies yourself, working with them hands-on rather than relying on what you hear, and understanding how others are using them.

Sufficient understanding means you have used these tools on your production work, can describe a task where they helped and a task where they did not, and can explain that judgement to your team. Deploying AI in your organizations requires carefully balancing between exploring new and better ways to do things and investing in doubling down on the ones you already have. Judgment and care are key. As a leader, we expect you to be taking ownership of connecting the inputs and outputs in your team or organization.”

Being close to the business is becoming a baseline expectation, says Amazon’s engineering leadership:

“We have also found that SDEs and SDMs who are closer to their products and businesses are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development. As Amazon has grown, we’ve seen some of our ICs and SDMs become less connected to their customers and business. We want to reverse this trend.

We recommend that ICs of all levels find ways to become deeply connected to your customers, and your team or org’s product direction. As always, the scope and depth of this ownership will increase as you become more senior.

For SDMs, we also recommend spending time making sure you’re close to your customers and business, and you’re helping the ICs in your organization to do the same.”

I interpret this as an expectation for software engineers to become product engineers who care about product, and can don a product management hat when needed. For platform teams, “customers” could include internal engineering teams – even so, platform engineers on this team need to be proactive in talking with those in-house devs. In my experience, devs on platform teams have always had direct lines with devs using their platform: it’s talking with external customers that most engineers have preferred to avoid, because it’s a hassle.

Engineering managers and product managers are no longer a middle layer between engineers and customers. It will be a big shift if all engineers are expected to be “deeply connected with customers”. Engineering managers (‘SDMs’ in Amazon lingo) and product managers will do less of that work, and the free time this creates could be occupied with building more software, becoming tech lead managers, or taking on larger teams.

Either way, engineering managers need to get back to being hands-on, and engineers need to become “engineer+product hybrids” if they want a long career at Amazon. We previously covered tactics to stay hands-on as an engineering manager.

I pay attention to how Amazon iterates on its engineering culture, processes, and compensation because the company is very good at getting a high return on investment (ROI) from its engineering org by spending as little as possible, while building a world-class engineering org. One takeaway from this is that AI removes any excuse for engineers and EMs not being extremely close to customers!

4. Microsoft issues new exit offers to engineers

Microsoft has announced a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to all software engineers below level 70, which is very high and encompasses a sizable chunk of the workforce; around 60,000 of the Windows maker’s 220,000 employees are eligible, Reuters reports. It’s Microsoft’s second bid to shed employees without layoffs in recent months. Here’s what happened last time:

  • Apr 2026: voluntary early retirement offered to 8,750 US employees

  • Jul 2026 : layoffs of about 4,800 people (~2% of workforce) – most of these being in the Xbox org

Based on that, it’s possible this large VEO is a sign of things to come. Companies often do VEOs when they want to reduce staffing numbers and have time to do so. People can leave on their own terms, and the more who accept a VEO, the smaller that overall layoffs should be – or perhaps none at all.

VEOs were offered to certain organizations and teams. From Microsoft’s announcement:

“[The Voluntary Exit Offer] gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. (...)Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.”

Reuters reports that orgs like Copilot, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices, are included, but marketing and security are not.

One surprise is that the offer extends to level 70. This is very senior at Microsoft, the Distinguished Engineer level on the IC track, and the VP of Engineering on the management track. Level 68 is already a partner, meaning those folks are also eligible.

The exit package is not tempting. Microsoft is not offering more than what these people would get if they were let go in layoffs, two current engineers at the company told me. Both of these engineers said that they’d much rather wait and see if there would be any layoffs involving them, as there’s no financial upside to accepting this VEO.

Also, the higher the level, the higher the compensation, and the exit offer doesn’t contain any farewell payment or “leaving bonus.” Unless folks in the upper echelons of seniority have a new job to start in 2027, they’ll be leaving money on the table compared to staying put.

Microsoft has been getting a lot bigger since before the pandemic. One “old timer” with 20+ years of tenure told me the company feels sluggish, and blames overhiring during the ZIRP and COVID-19 eras for excessive headcount growth. In 2016, Microsoft employed 116,000 staff, then 180,000 in 2019, and in 2020 it hit 220,000.

But revenue and profitability are at all-time highs. In all fairness, that excessive headcount growth was concurrent with rapid revenue growth, and since 2021, headcount has been flat at around 220,000 while revenue kept climbing. As visualized by Azeem Azhar in Exponential View:

Thanks to flat headcount and financial performance, revenue-per-employee is now also at an all-time-high, of $1.5M per year:

Based on the financials and profitability, everything looks great, so why is there any need for cuts?

This VOE may not be as drastic as it looks, and is almost certainly about specific Microsoft orgs fixing their budgets. MS has done plenty of layoffs, and it’s clear enough the company could make cuts again like in June with Xbox. Instead, it is making a Voluntary Exit Offer program, which is new for the company, and distinct from the retirement offer made earlier this year.

It’s clear the company wants certain orgs to become smaller, and that this VEO is an experiment on a pretty large scale. Microsoft’s own comms confirms the novelty:

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us [to Microsoft]. We’ll learn from it. (...) There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”

I talked with a former Microsoft executive who predicted that the leadership have modelled the “churn rate” – those accepting the package – and believes that between 5% and 10% of people will take the package. That’s 3,000-6,000, or 1.3-2.6% of Microsoft’s headcount, and a similar number to July’s job losses. Those departing would be self-selecting and therefore presumably content with the same package as they would get in the event of layoffs.

From the outside, Microsoft appears a single company, but inside, each org is its own thing of 10,000+ people. Many of them – like GitHub, Xbox, and LinkedIn – operate independently to a degree that might surprise some.

I’ll reserve judgement about this VEO until we see whether Microsoft announces layoffs, or the voluntary departures fulfil those “business needs.”

5. Security incidents continue

Since last week’s spate of high-profile security vulnerabilities, there have been more:

  • The Brotli remote execution CVE: Brotli is a compression library used at Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and others. The flaw allows an attacker to take over a service. Details

  • Another PHP remote code execution CVE. Just two days after the high-impact PHP2Shell patches, PHP warned of another important CVE, for which a fix is coming. PHP versions will need to be updated fast again.

  • Linux CVEs posted publicly. Several unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities were accidentally posted on the public kernel mailing list. Details.

  • Python Pillow CVE: a vulnerability inside the Python Pillow image library lets an attacker issue OS commands. Details

  • … and others I’ve doubtless missed.

At this rate, we might start getting “vulnerability fatigue” and become numb to critical security vulnerabilities unless they affect frameworks our applications use. To avoid that, it’ll be necessary for the industry to improve at coming up with and implementing security practices which work in a security environment where AI speeds up the discovery, publication, and exploitation of vulnerabilities.

Data Movement Strategies In System Design

ByteByteGo
Oct 29
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

Software systems don’t keep information in one place all the time. When a user makes a request to the system, it goes from the application to a server. A database might store the records needed to process it. Also, other components may need to know about any changes.

You need to move data to connect all these separate activities so that they can work as a coherent system.

To manage this movement of data, you need to make decisions about when and how information should travel within a system and outside it. This is where you have multiple strategies that can be used to handle data movement. In this article, we’ll look at the key strategies of data movement along with their benefits. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The source, consumer, and trigger of data movement

  • What is the pull approach

  • The polling approach

  • The push approach

  • The long polling approach

  • Continuous communication with SSE and WebSockets

  • The role of message queues

  • Change data capture for database changes

  • How to choose a data movement strategy

The Source, Consumer, and Trigger of Data Movement

Software engineering at Google & CS education with Titus Winters

Titus Winters shares lessons from engineering at Google’s scale and explores how AI is reshaping developer productivity and computer science education.

Gergely Orosz
Oct 29
 
READ IN APP
 

Before we start: I’m in SF this week and next, hosting these free-to-attend events (registration required). If you’re in the area, hopefully I'll see you at one of them:

  • The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged: Wednesday (4 Nov), 5pm-7:30pm. With Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). We still have space left, RSVP here.

  • System Update: Thursday (5 Nov) 5pm-8pm. We have some last spots left, RSVP here.

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress, take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3

• Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature to review PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It also supports stacked PRs. Check it out

• WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Give it a spin

In this episode

An engineer who helped create today’s software engineering curriculum now says to burn down almost all of it. What’s the cause of this contradiction? We find out from the lead author of Software Engineering at Google.

Titus Winters spent more than a decade at Google, where he led its readability program and built Abseil, Google’s open-sourced foundational C++ libraries. He is currently a Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe, where he focuses on developer experience and productivity.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Titus and I discuss how his team tackled a massive refactoring project across Google’s 250-million-line C++ codebase, why Google made testing mandatory, and his work on updating the ACM/IEEE undergraduate computer science curriculum guidelines.

We also explore why traditional productivity metrics miss some of AI’s biggest benefits, what needs to change in CS education, and how new engineers can stand out.

Takeaways from the conversation with Titus

Titus is a deep thinker and has worked on some very interesting projects. Here are 12 things that stick out to me from our chat.

1. Was refactoring 250M+ lines of C++ code the largest refactoring task of all time? This happened at Google in 2010, a few months after Titus joined the search giant. An internal email asked for volunteers to help clean up old C++ code, some of it written by the very first Googlers.

A team of a dozen people was assembled. Google had close to 250M lines of code at the time, edited by 10,000 engineers. Titus recalled the cleanup: “We were replacing the foundation of the Empire State Building. We were not allowed to close the building or block traffic. Oh, and we discovered nuclear waste in the basement.”

2. The refactoring was done with advanced language parsing techniques, long before LLMs existed. Back in 2010, there were no LLMs for this giant refactor. Here’s what the team did:

  • Parse: ran a MapReduce over the whole codebase. The mapper parsed every build target into an abstract syntax tree

  • Match: match exact call patterns in the tree

  • Code generation: generated edits to be made by the machine

  • Coexist: make the old API and new API work side-by-side

  • Shard: once the new API is ready to go, split the edits by directory, and send them out in batches

  • Block the old: make sure nobody copied the old pattern back into the code

  • Delete: remove the old API

The clang-format toolkit exists because Titus and his team needed it for this refactor.

3. Google made automated tests mandatory after Search could no longer ship regularly. Around 2007, Search, the flagship product, was unable to ship at a monthly cadence any more, and the best they could ship to production was quarterly.

Almost every change at Google touched Search’s code, even things like a change to Gmail. To clamp down, Google, as an org, mandated that every change was to be accompanied by a test. Over time, Search returned to its former higher cadence.

4. Google’s readability program might have been the largest educational program ever in tech. To make a code change at Google, two people need to sign off that change through a code review:

  • An “owner” of the file/project: someone on the team with domain knowledge

  • A “readability” reviewer: an engineer certified to be a “readability” expert in the given language that the change was made in

Google’s first engineer, Craig Silverstein, walked each new dev hire through their first change. Java teams turned this approach into mentoring, where experienced reviewers were assigned to review all changes in a round-robin fashion. And soon enough, a formalized readability program was built for all languages. When Titus left Google three months ago, 10,000+ engineers were enrolled in readability at any given time. Has there ever been a bigger engineering “classroom” anywhere else?

5. Fear is not an acceptable basis for engineering. Titus believes your codebase is unsustainable if it’s not possible to make a valuable change safely. There shouldn’t be fear about making a change to a codebase. Having the right “security nets” that catch errors is strategically very valuable because it enables teams to make changes without fear.

6. With AI, outages seem to be going up. Titus talks to engineers at other companies and it’s the same picture: code output is up hugely versus a year ago, and outages are also up about 30%, while the number of features shipped is static. It seems like treading water. From that angle, it’s not positive for AI; based on outages alone, the technology could be a negative.

7. On the other hand, AI makes ambitious projects possible that weren’t realistic without it. Titus is optimistic about AI as a net productivity boost, and reckons people are caring about the wrong things. He sees the real value of AI as not in repeating the same things as before at higher speed. Instead, it’s about doing things you never thought of before: projects so ambitious that they didn’t used to make sense!

8. Burn down the US undergrad CS curriculum (most of it). Titus was the only working engineer on the steering committee for the ACM/IEEE/AAAI CS curriculum guidelines in 2023, and believes the curriculum is hopelessly out of date. He accuses it of not having altered substantially since around 2000, while the industry has. Testing and verification are cited as mattering a lot more for new joiners, but they are absent from the curriculum.

Unless major changes are made to make it relevant, computer science enrollment could fall and software engineering programs that focus on practical dev skills will be attractive to students – this is Titus’s forecast.

9. “Middle group” of students struggle most with AI. Professors in CS programs tell Titus that students divide into three groups:

  • The best are better than ever and take full advantage of a patient, knowledgeable tutor, aka the AI

  • The middle: professors say that everyone below the “best” have collapsed: students below a B grade tend to not understand code at all

  • The weakest: they can catch up to the middle of the pack easier – mostly by producing slop with AI, though.

When I did a guest lecture at my alma mater, professors told me similar observations – how the “middle of the pack students,” by grades, have disappointingly low understanding of the subject, compared to former years.

10. Grading students’ prompts and tests is better than focusing on their code. Titus would focus on the thinking processes students put into building and validating software, not just the output.

11. “Remember Andrew’s axe” – advice for junior engineers. Andrew chops down a tree with an axe. Or did Andrew’s axe chop down the tree? Titus says Andrew is the one who did it, and the axe is only a tool for his will. Similarly with AI: it’s a tool for you to use, and anthropomorphizing this tool takes us out of that mindset.

12. To succeed, don’t copy what everyone else is doing! As our time came to an end, I asked Titus what he’d say to sophomore students. It’s a segment that did not make it into the podcast, but I’m adding it here!

“Most of my success in life has come from not doing the thing that everyone else is doing. It is really incredibly hard to stand out if you are just listening to what is a hot topic and chasing the same shiny thing that literally everyone else is doing.

My primary advice [is to] find something that you love that is not just the same thing that you assume is on everybody’s resume, and do a lot of that. Find a passion project, go really deep on it.

Like, ‘how do I use computing and AI vibe coded new generation techniques?’ ‘How do I solve this problem that matters a lot to me?’ ‘Or how do I express myself through a game or art?’ The more that you do [something] that’s uniquely you, the more that you stand out, and the more that you do, the more that you learn.”
