How Uber Built A Gateway For AI Agents To Access Tools

ByteByteGo
Oct 28
 
READ IN APP
 

Kalshi: Engineering for the Moments That Move Markets (Sponsored)

Markets don’t wait. On a prediction market, prices move in milliseconds, and every trade has to land the moment it happens. At the Agentic Data Summit on December 9, Batu Balimtas, Member of Technical Staff at Kalshi, takes you behind the scenes in Engineering for the Moments That Move Markets: Kalshi and Redpanda. Hear how Kalshi’s data infrastructure keeps pace when it matters most, and what it takes to run it in production. Catch Kalshi live at 12:00 PM PT. The summit is free and virtual and runs 8:30 AM–2:00 PM PT, so you can join for the sessions that matter most to you.

Save Your Seat

An off-the-shelf large language model can explain why there’s an error in your code. It can suggest possible causes. Or it can perform tasks like writing a database query. However, all this would be at a general level based on the model’s training. You cannot expect it to write answers based on your system’s internal workings.

This is handled using tools. Each tool is built for a specific job. But you can end up with lots of tools, especially when working in an enterprise setup. This is the situation the Uber engineering team faced.

To deal with this, they built the MCP Gateway. You can think of it as a shared platform that lets different AI agents find which tools are present and use them to perform their job. In this article, we’ll look at how Uber built this gateway in detail. Here’s what we will cover:

  • What are tools and why AI agents need them

  • The role of MCP at Uber

  • How the Uber MCP gateway is designed

  • How the gateway finds out the available tools

  • How does the MCP gateway work

  • How the MCP gateway deals with permission and access

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

Why AI Agents Need Tools

If you want a general-purpose LLM to write answers specifically for your current systems, you need to give it access to information about your system. For example, let’s say a developer asks an LLM-based AI assistant why XYZ service suddenly started failing. The answer is hidden in the system’s logs, deployments, metrics, and incidents. The LLM needs to access this information to be able to answer this question.

This is where we can create tools. You can think of a tool as an operation an AI application can execute. For example, you can have a tool to search logs. Retrieve incident details. Or check the status of a deployment. The model selects a tool and provides the necessary inputs. The application executes it and sends the result back to the model.

Many of these tools already exist as APIs. As you might already know, an API is an interface through which one program can request something from another program. For example, we can have a logging service that exposes an API. It takes the service name and time range as input and sends back all the log entries that fall within the range.

However, for an agent to use such a service, we need to describe what it does and what inputs it needs. This structured definition takes the form of a tool that the LLM application can use. Behind the scenes, the API performs the real search.

The Role of MCP at Uber

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. With MCP, you get a standard way for AI applications to find out available external capabilities and talk to them. Uber uses MCP for its tool ecosystem.

We must know three important terms to understand the role of MCP in a better way.

First, you have the MCP client. This is the component that sits inside an AI application. It communicates using MCP and handles various interactions, such as requesting the available tools. Or making calls to the selected tools.

Second, there is the MCP server. It exposes the capabilities (or tools) through MCP. In Uber’s case, the server shows the available tools and accepts any requests made to those tools.

Third, you have the MCP tool. This is the individual operation exposed by a server. You can also think of them as capabilities. One server can provide multiple tools.

MCP requires you to define the tools properly. This definition is made up of information such as name, description, and input schema. A schema provides the structure of data. Things like which fields are present, which are mandatory, and what types of values they can accept. For example, you can have a schema where service_name has to be a string and limit is an integer.

MCP uses a structured way to format a request or its parameters. Also, the corresponding result or error. The format is usually JSON-RPC 2.0. This standardization makes it easy to integrate stuff. You can have the same MCP client talk to different MCP servers.

However, this standardization doesn’t come for free. Someone has to decide which tools exist and where they run. Also, you need to track the ownership of the tools and how they work. Initially, the engineering teams within Uber built their own MCP integrations. The autonomy was great at a small level. But as adoption increased, it was obvious that each team was solving similar problems. For example, exposing tools. Managing connections. Dealing with permissions. And so on. To make things even more difficult, finding out which tools were available was difficult. Everything was scattered.

On top of all this, Uber’s existing service landscape brought another challenge. All the services in Uber didn’t talk to each other in the same way. Some used HTTP. Some used gRPC. And others used TChannel. For example, you might have an HTTP API use JSON and a gRPC API use Protobuf messages. You cannot simply forward an MCP request across these services without modifying the request format.

Therefore, Uber needed a common layer that could connect MCP clients to the tools. They also wanted this layer to handle shared discovery, security, and operational support. This layer is known as the MCP Gateway.

How the Uber MCP Gateway is Designed

The Uber MCP Gateway platform is divided into two main components: the MCP Registry and the Proxy Gateway. This separation helps Uber’s engineering team manage tool definitions and permissions independently.

Let’s look at both in detail.

MCP Registry

You can think of the MCP Registry as the control plane. It holds the catalog of MCP servers and tools. You can record the information needed to discover the tools and learn more about them in the registry.

The reason they call it the control plane is that the registry also manages the configuration. For example, you can enable or disable the tool from the registry. It is also a shared source of truth.

The Proxy Gateway

This is the data plane. It handles the real MCP requests while agents are doing their work.

The gateway identifies the requested tool. It applies the necessary controls and sends the request to the right service. Also, it returns an MCP-compatible result.

How Tools Are Discovered

You can’t manually create MCP integrations for 1000s of services. It’s a lot of work, and there are chances of errors. Uber has automated much of this work by using AutoCrawler.

AutoCrawler finds out existing APIs and MCP servers. It generates or retrieves their tool definitions and registers them in the MCP registry.

On a technical level, AutoCrawler is a distributed workflow system. It’s powered by Cadence. In this setup, you have a scheduled job start workflow that looks for any new services, APIs, or schema changes.

But how does AutoCrawler discover new things? It has two main discovery pathways:

From Existing API Definitions

Many APIs use an Internal Definition Language (IDL) to describe their APIs.

An IDL is a machine-readable description of a service interface. You can use it to specify operation names, request fields, and documentation comments. For example, you may have an API definition describe an operation named GetDeploymentStatus. It might take a deployment ID as input and return a status and timestamp.

AutoCrawler can read these definitions and then go through several steps.

First, it creates an MCP server representation for the service. It might also update an existing representation. Next, it pulls out method names, request and response structures. Then, it translates whatever it has found into tool schemas that MCP can make sense of.

AutoCrawler also uses an LLM to come up with better tool descriptions from the details it has extracted from the service. Finally, it stores these tool definitions in the registry.

As you can see, AutoCrawler is a good example of Uber’s no-code approach. Existing service contracts have enough information for the platform to build the MCP interface.

Discovering Native MCP Servers

Some services directly implement MCP. At Uber, these are called native MCP servers. These servers already have tool definitions. So less work for AutoCrawler to get those definitions.

Each native server emits a heartbeat metric. It signals the presence and readiness of the server. AutoCrawler keeps track of these signals. When it finds a server, it calls the server’s listTools operation. Once it finds the tools, it creates a proxy representation in the registry for all the tools and their schemas.

As you can see, both discovery pathways end up in the same catalog.

Discovering Tools vs Permission to Use Them

Uber made a design choice that newly discovered servers and tools start in a disabled state.

This means that automatic discovery only makes the capability visible to the platform. After this, the team that owns the service should review and enable the service to make it available for the agents. The choice to enable is an ownership decision. It’s better that the service team has the opportunity to check whether the tool description is correct.

The owner team can review the tool definitions and update them using the registry’s interface. Every modification is a new diff that should be approved. Only approved changes are deployed. Also, you can have owners roll back to the previous version if needed.

How Uber’s MCP Gateway Works

Once you have saved the tool configurations in the registry and have marked them as available, the data plane consumes these tool details to refresh its in-memory state. This happens at a fixed periodic interval.

The gateway uses the mappings at the time of request processing. The periodic refresh process makes sure that any new changes can take effect without the need to restart the service. Or redeploy it.

The gateway takes these configuration details and uses them to create virtual MCP servers. You can think of a virtual server as a logical MCP interface that exists inside the gateway. It’s made up of a collection of tools along with an endpoint for clients to reach those tools. For example, you can have a service called “logging” exposed on the endpoint “logging/mcp”.

To use the tool, the clients talk to this endpoint as an MCP server. You have a handler within the gateway that knows which tools are part of that server and how to reach the service that backs the tool.

To understand things in a better way, it’s good to follow the path of a request through the gateway.

Let’s say you have an AI agent that calls a tool backed by a gRPC service

  • First, the MCP request hits the gateway. The gateway finds the corresponding virtual server and the tool that is requested.

  • Next, the server handler uses an in-memory mapping to find out the downstream destination and operation. In this case, the downstream service is the service to which the gateway will send the request.

  • The handler converts the tool’s JSON arguments into a form that the service expects. For example, in the case of a gRPC operation, you have to serialize the request into Protobuf bytes.

  • Moving further, the service runs the operation and sends back the response.

  • Finally, the gateway converts the response into an MCP-compatible result and ships it back to the caller.

As you can guess, the same approach works for other types of services. For example, an HTTP backend receives an HTTP request. Or a TChannel service uses the TChannel or Thrift path.

How the Gateway Takes Care of Access

You can consider the gateway as a shared place to enforce access rules for all the tools.

The Uber engineering team uses their internal Access Control System to apply access rules and policies. These policies are based on the caller. You can have a human caller. A service. Or an AI agent. You can configure policies at the server level. Also, you can go as far as setting up specific policies for specific tools if needed. So the system provides a lot of flexibility.

This means that the platform supports authorization at the tool level. For example, you can have an incident management server expose tools for reading incidents and changing incident status. You can have a policy grant different access to those operations even though they are part of the same server.

The gateway can also redact responses for personally identifiable information (PII). Or any other sensitive data that may be present in the tool’s response.

For 3rd-party services such as Jira and Google, you need to have an additional identity check. This is because an internal Uber credential is different from a credential that might be accepted by a 3rd-party system. The gateway sends the caller’s internal user token to this service as part of its process flow. The 3rd-party service exchanges that token for the external auth token. Then, it sends the request to the external MCP server with that auth token.

As you can see, the responsibilities are divided. The gateway handles common access and execution details. The 3rd-party service takes care of the external stuff.

How the Uber MCP Gateway Deals With A Huge Catalog

The huge catalog of tools running at Uber can create a context problem for the MCP gateway.

You can have a gateway make 1000s of tools available, but an AI agent needs to have an efficient way to select the useful tools. This is because each tool definition takes up space in the model’s context window. You can think of this context window as the space available as part of the model’s input. This window has a limit. You also need it for other things like system instructions, conversation history, and results coming back from the tools.

If you have an application that loads tool descriptions and schemas for 1000s of tools in advance, they can take up a huge part of the context. Also, the amount of input that the model has to process shoots up. The same goes for tool responses. An API may send back a detailed object even when the task can be accomplished with just two fields.

To deal with these problems, Uber made three additions to the gateway:

  • Omni MCP helps agents discover capabilities gradually. It’s a single proxy server that lets MCP clients access any of the gateway’s servers with gradual discovery. It provides tools like “discover_server”, “discover_tools”, “get_tool_schema”, and so on.

  • Response Projection reduces the fields that are sent back in tool results. It’s a GraphQL-like pattern for MCP tools. You inject a new field in the tool request that tells the gateway which fields should be part of the response. The gateway removes the other fields.

  • Code Mode lets coding agents work with results using shell commands and files.

Conclusion

Building the MCP Gateway has changed how AI agents operate at Uber in a big way.

It began as a fragmentation problem. You had dozens of teams independently wiring up MCP integrations. There was inconsistent tooling. No shared security guarantees. Also, duplicated infrastructure. Now, everything is a unified platform that can be scaled. Any team can plug into this platform within minutes.

The core philosophy that drove Uber’s team was that existing APIs are the fastest way to let AI agents access the tools. They didn’t want the teams to rewrite their services to make them fit for the gateway. The MCP gateway does the heavy lifting.

The key takeaway for developers is that the hardest part of building agentic systems is not the AI. You should worry more about building the right connective tissue. Things like discovery, security, and reliability are very important in a production environment.

References:

  • Designing MCP Gateway Uber’s MCP Management Platform

  • Model Context Protocol

👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

AI SRE: what is it, how could it change on-call – and does it work?

“AI SRE” is fast becoming a trending term fueled by flashy demos from vendors, but has an AI SRE ever really been on-call while engineers slept? Deepdive

Gergely Orosz and Jessica Salmon
Oct 27
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Before we start: I’m in San Francisco this week and also next week. On Wed, 4 November, I’m hosting The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged at the iconic SFJazz Club, featuring a rare conversation with Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). It’s free to attend with registration, sign up here.

In May 2025 at Microsoft’s annual BUILD conference, the tech giant introduced “Azure SRE Agent” with an onstage demo in which an alert fired and the AI SRE Agent went to work on identifying the root cause, and then shipped a fix, all without having to wake up a human dev oncall.

Watching this demo, the whole thing felt artificial to me, and I failed to imagine any engineering team at Microsoft – or anywhere else! – letting an AI make production decisions with no human oversight that could potentially cause a worse outage. And sure enough, after last year’s BUILD I heard no more about “SRE agents” at Microsoft or elsewhere – until recently, that is.

Now, I do hear it being mentioned: OpenAI built an AI SRE bot called Sevbot, and last month, an engineer at ING bank told me they’re working on their own, in-house AI SRE. Just as visibly, at tech conferences I’ve attended, AI SRE vendors’ stands have been popping up in numbers.

To find out what’s going on, we reached out with Jessica to three of the most popular AI SRE startups/AI incident platforms to hear directly from them: Rootly, incident.io, and ResolveAI (note: I’m an investor in incident.io). Thanks for all the input!

Today, we cover:

  1. Why is AI SRE “hot”? Incidents and pages are trending upward, thanks to AI agents speeding up at shipping code to production. It only makes sense to invest in better oncall tooling.

  2. What does “AI SRE” mean? It’s mostly about doing incident investigation much faster, and inside of Slack. Whether “AI SREs” should make code changes is debated.

  3. Building an investigation agent. Fanning out multiple agents is common, as is the practise of engineers steering them in Slack or Teams. A “context layer” with a knowledge graph and memory is used for better investigation outcomes. Several tech companies built their own investigation agents instead of relying on vendors.

  4. Making agents accurate. Helpful approaches include verifying incident hypotheses with adversarial agents and a mix of models, as well as running evals and backtesting. However, measuring “accuracy” of AI SREs is tricky and highly specific to each company, and even engineering team.

  5. Making agents fast & affordable. Everyone wants fast, cheap, and accurate AI SREs, but there are tradeoffs. Model routing, lean prompts, and tracking cache hit rate are ways to engineer a system with the right tradeoffs for your constraints.

  6. How long until autonomous agents? The fully autonomous agents demoed on conference stages are still not a reality, but AI agents triaging pager calls – and silencing unimportant ones – is becoming more common. Interestingly, there’s not been much change in this area from how Meta operated its own systems with AI two years ago.

  7. What’s changing for on-call engineers? A new category of AI-related outages is appearing, and engineers should eventually get hit with fewer pages, but the incidents that do reach engineers will be hard. There’s a deskilling risk, and it could be smart to train oncall with incident response simulations like those from Uptime Labs.

1. Why is AI SRE “hot”?

A year back, there was little to no buzz about AI SREs, but that’s all been changing.

The main driver seems to be that there’s a lot more code deploys. Almost all tech companies have seen their PR frequency double in a year due to AI agents. Let’s do some basic “reliability math”:

i = c x p:
Incident rate = [Change rate] x [Probability]

C = number of changes per unit time
P = probability a single change introduces failure

This says that if we have few deployments (low change rate) and high confidence that each deploy works (low probability of failure), then that is a pretty stable system. But with AI agents, deploy frequency is up and the incident rate is likewise increasing at most companies.

We know that C (the number of changes in a given timeframe) is up twofold or more on last year at many companies, and will probably climb higher. Data from Rootly shows that pages are also up from a year ago, and outside-business-hours pages have nearly doubled:

Broadly, there’s two approaches to lowering P (incident failure rate probability):

  1. Better pre-deploy verification: more testing & verification loops

  2. Learn from incidents: make the system more resilient

Most AI SRE vendors are well placed to learn from incidents and act upon them. For example, here’s Rootly’s high-level strategy for more resilient systems:

2. What does “AI SRE” mean?

“AI SRE” looks on its way to becoming the agreed term for AI-augmented oncall tooling, even though we’ve not spoken to a single person who likes it – and we agree.

AI SRE vendors themselves don’t like it. When we talked with incident.io, Resolve, and Rootly for this article, the reply was that, unfortunately, they’ve not come up with anything better and so this name has come to stick instead. Alternative names proved less sticky even though they’re less inaccurate, like “autonomous reliability agents”, “automated remediation agents”, and “automated incident investigation agents.”

A reason “AI SRE” is less than ideal is as simple as the fact that a site reliability engineer (SRE) does a lot more than just deal with oncall alerts! They work on making a system more reliable in its entirety and a good chunk of that work happens before and after outages.

Despite all that, this article is going with the flow and using “AI SRE” because there’s not much choice, while covering oncall and incident handling tools that are AI-augmented/AI-powered.

We cover more on the SRE profession and reliability engineering in a deepdive with Dave Connor, who worked at Google when the term ‘SRE’ was coined.

AI SRE tools mostly help with the investigation phase of incidents. Tools like Rootly, incident.io, and ResolveAI are most helpful after an alert has fired and an engineer starts investigating. Pre-AI, this investigation phase involved:

  • Alert details: inspect the alert and try to figure out what it means

  • Dashboards: check custom dashboards to confirm whether there’s an alert, which systems are impacted, and where the root cause investigation should start, if so

  • Runbooks: consult runbooks and follow the steps to remedy the issue, if it’s a common one

  • Logs/observability: look through the logs of observability systems like Datadog, Sentry, Honeycomb, etc

These days, AI tools have gotten pretty good at all these tasks if they have sufficient data access. Of the three vendors we talked with, all do their investigations with AI. When building in-house AI SRE tools, starting at the investigation phase is a no-brainer:

Most AI SRE tools speed up the investigation of an incident. incident.io’s agent orchestrator does something similar to when an oncall engineer opens eight tabs to look through what systems might have issues:

  • Orchestration: the main agent decides to kick off an investigation

  • Subagents: it fans out investigation work to subagents which report on progress

  • Heuristics: the orchestrating agent can make speculative calls, then use heuristics to decide where to go deeper

There’s a lot of value in having an oncall engineer join the incident channel roughly five minutes after an alert fires, and to have a summary of investigations by AI agents. It gives the oncall dev a sense of what might be happening, instead of having to do all the “shovel work.”

AI SREs typically interact with devs in Slack. At startups that use Slack for comms, Slack is also the place to coordinate incidents; even pre-AI, it was common to open a dedicated Slack channel for an incident. Most AI SRE tools have a Slack bot in the incident channel; incident.io’s bot sits in the incident channel the whole time and takes steering instructions from engineers (look at the status of a specific system, ask it to dig up specific logs, etc.)

AI SRE tools require a high level of trust, which is a reason to build in-house. For these agents to be effective, they need access to telemetry, observability, logs, even the version control system because the more data they can access, the more effective they are. As Sam Newman writes in his book, ‘Building Resilient Distributed Systems’:

“For tools like incident.io’s AI SRE to work, they need access to information. This means that they will need broad access to a lot of valuable data if you want them to be effective. If the agent can’t see your telemetry data, then it can’t slice and dice that data for you. If it can’t look at your source code repository, then it can’t spot recent commits that may have caused the issue. This does mean that you need a high degree of trust in the vendor creating and running the agent.”

But how much do you trust a third-party vendor with all your data; potentially even a readonly version of your sanitized production database, which could come in handy for some investigations? The larger the company, the less likely that access to highly sensitive data will be granted. The trust issue is a major driver in why many mid-size-and-above companies build their own AI SRE tools.

Even if a vendor offers zero data retention (ZDR), there’s still a risk that its system could be compromised and leak information. Also, a vendor offering ZDR could be at a disadvantage when improving the system, compared to an in-house AI SRE tool that it’s possible to train on the data.

Our take is that AI SRE vendors are likely to become more capable than home-grown solutions because AI SRE startups obsess about better tooling fulltime; success depends on it. At larger companies, an AI SRE tool is more of a novel side project; engineers initially get excited but then move on to newer projects.

Should AI SREs only mitigate, or also remediate? Once the root cause analysis of an outage is done, and the AI SRE agent has helped to mitigate it, is the work complete? On one hand, the AI SRE tool typically also has access to the codebase, so should be able to come up with code-fix suggestions. On the other hand, pre-AI, you hardly ever saw an SRE team raise pull requests to fix the root causes of outages because they didn’t have the context or expertise for systems someone else built. But with AI, context can be passed on and expertise in writing code is pretty common for AI agents.

We asked the three AI SRE startups how they approach writing code to fix root causes, post-incident. They have different ways:

  • Handing off PRs to coding agents. incident.io is focused on passing incident context to engineers’ existing coding agents. The company built and demoed autonomous PR creation at its annual conference last year, but cofounder Chris Evans told us that customers generally prefer to use their own coding setups. The focus is therefore on giving agents the context they need to help engineers implement a fix.

  • A hybrid approach at ResolveAI. The tool writes simple PRs itself and hands over larger changes to the customer’s coding agents.

  • Intend for agents to autonomously merge PRs at Rootly. Their vision is to get to a point where their agent drafts a PR, and another agent judges whether it’s safe to merge, and when deemed safe, the merge happens automatically. If the merge is deemed risky, the oncall engineer still gets woken up. As yet, all PRs raised happen after a human has approved them.

3. Building an investigation agent

All three vendors we talked to have rebuilt their investigation agent at least once because integrating AI into oncall looks simple, but that’s not the case. For example, ResolveAI built three different architectures in two years:

Scripted workflow. In 2024, models could not yet reliably chain tool calls. The startup built a pipeline of specific prompts like: “classify the alert“ → “gather logs+metrics“ → “extract insights” → “rank hypotheses.” This pipeline handled common incidents well, but did poorly when incidents did not “fit the script”.

Single agent with a knowledge graph. In 2025 when tool calling with AI agents became reliable, a primary agent took the alert → looked at a graph of services/dependencies/runbooks/deployments → decided what to do next. Overall, the accuracy improved but new problems appeared:

  • Context rot: for long, multi-service incidents, the agent ran into context saturation (the “dumb zone” as discussed on the Pragmatic Engineer podcast episode with Dex Horthy). It started to request data it already had and to contradict its own conclusions.

  • Self-confirmation: the agent was tasked to grade hypotheses it came up for likely causes of incidents. The agent almost always confirmed its first suspicion and didn’t examine its conclusion.

  • Lack of ‘memory’: lessons from past investigations didn’t carry over to new ones.

Multi-agent system. In 2026, the team came up with three different agent roles:

  • Investigator: chases one hypothesis after another

  • Verifier: challenges the conclusions of investigators. It’s structurally independent of investigators to avoid self-confirmation

  • Communicator: agent updates stakeholders

The Resolve team told us they find this system to be the most reliable and resilient in incident investigations.

A typical investigation

At a high level, all three AI SRE startups follow similar steps for dealing with investigations:

  1. Trigger: an alert fires or an engineer declares an incident

  2. Orientation: pull in relevant data like telemetry and logs to find out what’s changed recently, like deployment and feature flags

  3. Fan out: kick off parallel investigative agents.

  4. Verify: challenge the conclusions of investigative agents

  5. Report: update Slack and other communication channels

  6. Steer: engineers give input to the agent, usually via Slack. This spawns more “fan out” investigations

  7. Hand off: an engineer or coding agent takes on suggested mitigation actions, like making a code change, restarting a system, etc.

There’s plenty of nuance in how to implement each step: our three vendors often do so in distinct ways! Here are tactics for each step:

  • Trigger: how do you categorize alerts: do you give fixed buckets for the agent (e.g. “needs human attention”, “can wait for business hours”, “noise”), or have the agent come up with a hypothesis for the cause before paging a human?

  • Orient: do you measure the potential impact of the page (which can add latency), follow different rules based on the service impacted, or pull in a larger context graph?

  • Fan out: do you fan out by hypothesis/potential failure type, or with as many agents as makes sense? What about long-running agents; do you wait for them, or limit tool-calling depth, or the cost of an investigation agent run?

  • … and so on for other steps. You’ll want to decide on tradeoffs between latency, accuracy, and cost.

Context layer, knowledge graphs, memory

AI SRE tools need some kind of understanding of what the production system looks like: how systems are connected, the dependencies, and what caused things to go down previously. All three AI SRE tools build some kind of “context layer” to help the agent figure out root causes of an incident faster:

  • Rootly calls its Atlas: a combination of a knowledge graph, memory, and AI connectors

  • incident.io calls its Nexus: a combination of catalog, code, telemetry, and past incidents

  • Resolve calls its HiveMind: a combination of context, investigation skills, memory, and actions

Generalizing a bit, all three of these context layers are made up of a knowledge graph, memory, and tools.

Knowledge graph

This is a graph of:

  • Services

  • Data stores

  • Cloud resources

  • Deployments

  • Runbooks

  • Past incidents

  • … and other relevant resources or sources of information

This is not something that only vendors build; practically any team building AI tools can come up with it. For example, Uber built a neat in-house knowledge graph that’s used by most of their AI systems, which we cover in the podcast episode ‘Uber’s AI infra from the inside.’

Memory

Memory is the system for storing information from past investigations. Agents can use this layer to steer the current investigation and memory provides information like:

  • “When latency spikes on payments, the root cause is more often than not with the connection pool”

  • “This specific alert is typically noise the first hour after a deploy from a specific service”

  • etc.

All three AI SRE startups have their own memory layers, but each implements it slightly differently. For example, Rootly has the concepts of:

  • “Activated” memory notes: a note earns its spot in a more important memory note after playing a useful role in an incident, or someone activates it manually

  • “Quarantined” memory notes: if a note is contradicted, it gets quarantined to not be used in the future. Systems keep changing, and this is one way to not feed stale information to the agent

Is it a good idea to pool customers’ incident data? AI SRE vendors have the advantage that they observe more incidents – and very different ones – via customers. Among our three vendors, Rootly is the only one that allows customers to opt into pooling their data in return for getting a hopefully improved agent.

Rootly’s idea is to build a kind of “Stack Overflow for AI SREs” internally. The idea is that Company A’s retrospective – scrubbed of sensitive details – might help Company B resolve an incident faster. Cofounder JJ Tang:

“Most vendors in our space promise your data stays siloed forever. We think that’s the wrong default for operational data. For example, an outage caused by a bad Redis config isn’t a trade secret.”

Sharing of confidential data is a tricky topic. Rootly says it gives customers granular control over what is shared and excluded, and can access shared records and remove them. The scrubbing code is not currently open-sourced, which the company plans to change.

Our take is that benefiting from a “knowledge base” is promising, but contributing to a broader vendor knowledge base needs to be done carefully. Responsible vendors will make contributions easy and transparent. Just ensure that when contributing data, anything confidential is scrubbed first.

Tools

Agents use tools, connectors, plugins, and AI skills to connect to data sources during an investigation. This is pretty similar to how any AI vendor is integrated into a company with the right connectors. Needless to say, all AI vendors expose MCP interfaces, and offer Claude Code/Codex plugins for easy integration with other internal services.

Agents in the Slack channel

AI SREs typically interact with devs in Slack during an incident. Teams is also supported by all three AI SRE startups, and Rootly also supports GChat, but most startups are on Slack. It’s interesting that Slack is becoming the preferred choice for human-to-agent communication of most tech companies.

There are a few challenges these tools need to solve:

  • Length of updates. How concise or verbose should updates by the AI SRE tool be? incident.io played a lot with getting this right: they learned that being too concise makes devs not trust the agent (too few details), whereas being too lengthy can be annoying

  • When to speak up? Rootly designed its agent to be predominantly quiet and to only post when:

    • a question in the channel goes unanswered

    • a stakeholder joins without context

    • someone declares “mitigated” without proof

    • a risky action is announced with no rollback plan

How in-house teams build AI SREs

Lots of medium-sized and larger tech companies build AI SREs in-house, and the big benefit is that they can expose internal context a lot more freely to their agent than to a vendor. My sense is that the AI SREs built by different companies end up being pretty similar in capabilities and structure to those that vendors build.

The AI SRE is a subset of Monzo’s cloud agent, which calls its cloud coding agent ‘Project Chip’. This is the high-level architecture:

Agent Chip is a general, in-house, engineering agent that can be triggered from Slack, Linear, GitHub, and other internal systems. When an incident occurs, Agent Chip has ‘Agent Chip Incident Mode’ invoked and it pulls together context from across systems, surfaces possible causes, and can draft a fix.

Other places have in-house AI SREs:

  • OpenAI: its tool is ‘Sevbot’. It collects details, determines possible mitigations (but never executes any), answers devs’ questions in a Slack channel, and can apply mitigations when instructed

  • Stripe: built its own incident investigation agent that runs on each outage. A simpler run (that tends to collect necessary signals to investigate the outage) takes three minutes, on average. A more thorough deep investigation is 14 minutes long, on average.

  • Google: SREs use ‘ProdAgent’ (Google’s internal agentic incident management framework) within Gemini CLI. It functions like get_incident_details, causal_analysis, timeseries_correlation, log_analysis and others. ProdAgent doesn’t generate code, it only suggests using tools exposed via MCP, like borg_task_restart (Borg being Google’s infra management platform). ProdAgent has policy enforcement and audit trails. It seems less polished, but is built to minimize the risk of messing up production: more scripts, less LLM determinism!

4. Making agents accurate

An engineering challenge of building AI SRE tools is that they need to be right most of the time, even when built on models prone to confabulation and which change often.

Verification

incident.io, Rootly, and ResolveAI all verify the RCA of the investigating agents with a step that challenges hypotheses and checks all claims are backed by sources. All are clear that the model which formed the hypothesis isn’t responsible for verifying the output.

Adversarial agents: incident.io uses these to fact check the claims that led the investigating agent to a leading theory. If it finds a claim with no supporting evidence like a metric or query, it downgrades it: e.g., an uncited “we definitely think it’s the database” becomes “we think it could be the database”. They grade each hypothesis on a five-level scale: speculation, pattern match supported by context, validated by system state, and validated alternatives ruled out. This approach is informed by a mental model of labelling findings in a live investigation used by the founders’ Monzo colleague, Oliver Beattie, who used to communicate RCA confidence in live incidents.

Separate verifier agent: ResolveAI uses an agent that applies adversarial pressure on the conclusions of the investigating agents, and checks for citations. They used to have the same agent that investigated an incident to also verify the output, but in practice, this sometimes led to the agent latching onto a theory early on, then finding evidence that confirmed the theory and concluding the investigation with the wrong answer. They reported a twofold jump in accuracy after they adopted their multi-agent architecture, which has separate investigation and verification agents.

Mixture of models: Rootly uses a mixture of models and code to verify leading theories. They use code for verification because models will produce a plausible explanation for anything.

They use a model to mark each hypothesis as being supported, refuted, or inconclusive, and give a confidence score. They don’t give the model tool access so that it can only score what the investigation already found. Rootly considers a confidence score of 85% to be high for a response.

They then do a pass with a model that argues against each surviving hypothesis on whether the timing and mechanism checks out, if it looks coincidental, or if there are better explanations. It can adjust conclusions from pass-one and use code to cap the confidence score of any hypothesis lacking decisive evidence.

Rootly relies on code to settle the verification stage. The final code check applies four checks to the evidence: has the confidence threshold been met, did the decisive test run, did the decisive evidence come from at least two different tools observing the system, and was a specific cause found?

If all four are positive, they label it “root cause identified”. Otherwise, it fails and is labeled “Inconclusive — needs human”, with the leading hypothesis marked “suspected, not confirmed”.

Evals

A key engineering challenge of building AI SRE tools is knowing if the system is improving or degrading over time, especially as they’re built on top of models. This is not unique to AI SRE tools, but to any software running on top of LLMs. As Sam Newman writes in Building Resilient Distributed Systems (emphasis ours):

“Aside from the fact that LLMs are nondeterministic, small changes in models can also lead to quite different behavior.

I’ve seen reports where a model has started behaving differently, without any major change in behavior being flagged by the vendor. Additionally, moving to a newer version of a model can fundamentally change how your prompts may be handled.

It is therefore vital to have a good set of tests to validate that the AI portions of your code are behaving appropriately, and this should be a mix of traditional functional tests, together with the use of AI evaluation tools (evals). You want to make sure that when the unexpected occurs, you get surprised first, rather than your users.”

A live incident is certainly not the time to find out that a change to an AI SRE tool or model has degraded its ability to reach an accurate root cause. The vendors we spoke to all run evals to test how accurately their AI SRE tools respond to incidents. For example, incident.io told us that producing an RCA is the result of up to hundreds of model calls, and that prompt-level evals are not enough. Cofounder Chris Evans:

“Evals are like a bunch of unit tests around individual prompts. We can be confident those are working, but when you assemble the whole, how do you know whether you’ve gone from a problem to the diagnosed cause being correct? That was the single hardest thing.”

Chris told us that measuring the accuracy of their system is one of the main challenges of building the investigations tool. Their solution is to use backtesting, which re-runs the investigations tool for previous incidents and tests that it reached the right outcome.

As with human engineers, AI SRE tools can only know after the fact whether they’ve correctly identified and fixed an incident. When a user edits an AI-generated postmortem or talks about the resolved incident in Slack, they give context that allows the AI SRE tool to know if its diagnosis and response were right and useful. This is how the tool understands the correct answer.

After every incident, incident.io grades the investigation against what a responding engineer said caused it. This engineer’s context becomes the “ground truth” and they give the investigation a score:

  • 100%, bullseye: acting on the investigation’s diagnosis fixes the incident

  • 65%, on target: right, but one piece is missing

  • 35%, miss: the right area, but the wrong course of action

  • 0%, nowhere near: points to a different part of the system

incident.io backtests to see how a new change affects their system, like when a new model affects accuracy. Each model release has the potential to improve or degrade the system. incident.io told us they have experienced new model releases negatively impacting accuracy. Chris Evans, cofounder:

“If OpenAI brings out a new model, we wonder whether it makes things better or worse. It turns out that in the past, when new models came out, accuracy got worse. [For teams] who don’t have this ground-truthing ability, you truly are operating on vibes”.

To backtest, they run the old and new versions of their system across a set of incidents and re-run each incident several times to account for model variations. For each one, they go back to the starting time with only the evidence that was available then to check that it reached ground truth.

Freezing the incident in time is a big challenge. A backtest needs to give the investigation all the context that the tool had when the incident started: the alert, telemetry, and the PR. However, because the backtest is being run in the future, there’s already a lot of pollution which can skew the backtest result, like the final postmortem, and the Slack context which helped to establish the ground truth in the first place.

Accuracy

A lot of the work that goes into AI SRE tools is in making them as accurate as possible, and measuring that accuracy. As mentioned, Rootly, incident.io, and ResolveAI’s tools do this by grounding investigative agents with a context layer and using evals.

It makes sense why accuracy is such a prominent metric for AI SRE tools, as no engineering team would trust a tool that regularly misdiagnoses incidents. When we spoke to incident.io, cofounder Chris Evans showed us the internal dashboard for Investigations running on incident.io’s own incidents, which targets 80%+ accuracy.

Despite many vendors using accuracy as a metric of how well their system works, it alone isn’t the most important – or even a stable – one.

Accuracy scores depend on the systems it is measured on: It’s important to remember that just because one vendor or customer has a great accuracy score, such accuracy isn’t guaranteed to be repeated everywhere else. Rootly told us that when they replay their own incidents, it shows how the agent performs on its own stack of AWS, Datadog, Sentry and GitHub, whereas customers run every combination of Kubernetes, Grafana, clouds and home-grown tooling. So, vendors use different strategies to tackle this: Rootly runs custom evals per customer, incident.io will backtest on request for changes in their customers’ systems, like connecting with new telemetry. Even with these measures, an accuracy metric in one place isn’t automatically the same on another system.

What’s considered accurate varies from customer to customer. The perception of accuracy can be subjective. incident.io shared that they see instances where they graded something as accurate but a customer didn’t.

5. Making agents fast & affordable

All three vendors said the order of importance for engineering teams is speed (latency) and accuracy, followed by cost.

Latency

Downtime is expensive and AI SREs that rapidly come up with mitigation strategies save money by reducing Time To Mitigate (TTM). For example, this is how Stripe measured its in-house agent’s latency:

Here’s data on how long things take for Rootly:

So, how to further reduce latency? Here are some techniques which different vendors mentioned:

  • Parallel fan-out. An obvious approach involving launching parallel agents to do standalone investigations.

  • Speculative calls: incident.io fetches data that might be needed later, to reduce latency.

  • Narrow the search: using tools like the knowledge graph to point to areas/systems where the root cause is more likely located. It’s an area where Rootly’s approach to pooling data from customers into their Atlas context layer can be helpful.

  • Show partial results. Start showing details of longer investigations, and allow engineers to steer the agent

  • Use smaller models. Smaller models can be faster and cheaper

Model routing

Which model to use for investigative tasks? This can be tricky to decide!

Rootly created an open-sourced SRE-skills-bench to evaluate AI models on SRE work, and used this measurement until February of this year, when Gemini 3.1 Pro saturated it, scoring 98%. Here’s what they learned after tracking top models for several months:

  • SRE work is different from coding work, and the “best” coding models aren’t always the “best” SREs

  • The “best” model depends on the task. Storage, networking, and identity problems each have different leaders at different price points

Also, moving to a new model can lead to regressions. Chris Evans at incident.io told us that moving to a new model for the orchestration LLM did reduce accuracy, which was caught by evals. It’s common for AI SRE vendors to do automatic model routing based on the task.

Rootly gave more details on how it does model routing:

  • Classify: a classifier labels each step within an investigation

  • Route: the best model for the job is selected for specific steps

For example, the category of correlating logs is pattern matching, which is done quickly and accurately by small models. However, challenging a hypothesis is complex work, so top reasoning models are used. Around 70% of investigation steps run on small, fast, cheap models, the Rootly team told us.

Cost control

The Rootly team also revealed their strategy for cost control:

  • Model routing: choosing cheaper reasoning models when using a more expensive one would not have advantages. Selection is based on their benchmark data

  • Lean prompts: an agent doing an investigation connects to dozens of external tools through connectors, but loading every tool schema into every prompt is expensive. Rootly uses tool search, and lazy loading of large schemas

  • Cache hit rate: prompts are structured so their stable calls get reused across calls. The team tracks cache hit rate as a first-class cost metric

  • Zero-token steps: anomaly detection runs using “old school” code

  • Hard budget caps: every investigation runs within fixed limits for tool calls, model usage, and rounds. This limits the load upon customers’ observability APIs in terms of how often they get hit

Build vs buy?

With AI, it’s become a lot easier to build any tool in-house. We’ve seen tech companies build their own coding harnesses – and covered Ramp’s Inspect in-depth. Several companies are also building their own AI SRE.

Reasons why companies build, based on what we’ve gathered:

  • Data access and trust. An efficient AI SRE has access to as much context as possible, including information that some companies would not want to expose to a third-party vendor, like readonly access to the sanitized production DB. The larger the company, the less likely it wants to allow third parties to have this level of access.

  • Control over model providers. Companies that operate open models, or run their own inference might want the AI SRE to use those specific models. It might be easier to build your own AI SRE than try to wire your models into a third party’s.

  • You could extend your in-house cloud agent. Monzo’s general coding agent (Agent Chip) has an ‘Agent Chip Incident Mode’ which handles incident management. Why have a separate tool when your coding agent can take on some more incident management work?

  • It’s a way for engineers to learn and upskill. Building an in-house incident management platform is a great way for the devs building it to become more hands-on with AI engineering. Plus, even if the company moves to a vendor in the future, having an in-house AI SRE system gives them the upper hand in negotiations.

Below are reasons why companies buy, based on the three AI SRE vendors we’ve talked with:

  • A system guaranteed to work. Building in-house risks a system that operates on “vibes” and not measurement. AI SRE vendors spend a lot of time and effort measuring efficiency, and can give hard numbers on how efficient it is.

  • Models change fast. Keeping up with the latest models – and re-running internal evals – is the bread-and-butter of AI SRE vendors, but it might be something that in-house teams don’t do as often.

  • Cost control. AI SRE vendors do optimizations to reduce the investigation cost per incident – something that in-house teams might not focus as much on.

  • ROI. To build in-house, you need to dedicate engineering hours to building it and also pay operating costs. Buying a vendor solution may be cheaper.

  • Main mission vs side project. For a vendor, the AI SRE product is their full focus. For a company, it’s a side project that gets less attention, and one which engineers eventually move on from.

6. How long until autonomous agents?

The vision of AI SRE vendors is for AI SREs to autonomously handle some incidents, so that oncall engineers don’t need to be woken up outside of business hours for an incident that agents can handle with high confidence.

But as things stand today, practically no one runs fully autonomous AI SRE agents in production. One exception is at AI SRE vendors: for example, Rootly internally runs a “no human first-responder” AI SRE, and allows it to push changes straight to production. Here’s how they define levels of AI SRE autonomy:

It’s becoming common for AI agents to triage alerts. All three vendors have functionality that lets an AI agent do this and then decide whether to close it as noise, postpone until business hours, or escalate to a human.

AI agents acting autonomously happens with heavy guardrails. It’s still very risky to let an AI agent take action on anything that touches production. AI SRE startups give customers the option to trust agents to do pre-approved actions:

  • Rootly: allow agents to execute a list of pre-approved fixes, like rolling back a recent change or turning off a feature flag

  • ResolveAI: guardrails can be defined per service. Guardrails list what the agent can do on its own, what needs approval, and what it must never do.

All tools that Google’s ProdAgent has access to are labeled as one of these:

  • ‘Safe’ – e.g. readonly tools

  • ‘Reversible’ – e.g. rollbacks, feature flags turned on or off

  • ‘Destructive’ – e.g. deleting data

Policies define the category of tools an agent can use, and what approval it needs. For reversible or destructive tools, I’d assume that most teams want human approval to run!

Interestingly, Meta was doing all the above in 2024 with much less advanced AI models. In December that year, the social media giant shared details about its autonomous reliability agents, back when the state-of-the-art AI model was Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Their system achieved a 60% time reduction in mitigating incidents. The company already had the concept of self-healing systems and a rigid process on how systems can “graduate” in autonomy levels.

7. What is changing for on-call engineers?

Fully autonomous AI SREs are not yet a reality, but modern AI SRE tools are changing how engineers handle oncall rotations. Here are our observations of what this may mean for engineers:

Oncall rotation is staying for the foreseeable future. Similarly to how software engineering teams are not going anywhere at “AI-pilled” companies like Anthropic, all the AI SRE startups told us that oncall rotations remain a thing at the businesses they work with.

There’s a new category of AI-related outage. AI systems are being deployed to production, and – naturally – they are breaking. Data from Rootly has a few interesting findings:

All incidents are up 2.5x overall, with AI-related incidents up by 4.5x, model provider-related incidents up 13x, and MCP-related incidents up 14x. Production AI systems need to prepare for model providers being down, and MCP systems might need to put more thought into reliability.

For devs, orchestrating agents becomes more common during outages than utilizing personal technical skills. Chris Evans at incident.io compared this change to a broader one within software engineering:

“This new world of oncall skews towards people who are good at managing and delegating. It will be much less about the raw technical skills of ‘can I go into Prometheus and write the right PromQL query?’ Being good at writing PromQL will be undifferentiated in the same way as me writing a function in Go is undifferentiated today.

However, knowing what to build or what to query or how to interpret responses with agents: these will become more important. Oncall will become more like working with other experts in the room, similar to how software engineering is becoming this kind of setting.”

Humans continue to make judgment calls. Steven Karis at ResolveAI:

“In production operations, a lot of decisions are ultimately judgment calls: what is the impact I’m willing to make on my customers? Is five minutes of a hard outage worth being fully operational after those five minutes? Or is 30 minutes of degraded performance better? This is something that you as a business have to decide.”

Fewer pages to hit engineers, eventually. Rootly told us that seven out of 10 alerts within its own team were closed without human intervention in the last 12 months, and out-of-hours pages were cut by around half. Of course, their product is the AI SRE, so they are far more “AI-pilled” and experimental with this than most places are, and could be months or years ahead of the broader industry with these numbers. But if it can automate incident management and reduce oncall noise, there should be demand for its product.

We suspect all AI SRE vendors and tools treat noisy alert reduction as a priority, and will start to automate “simple” incidents. Eventually, engineers should receive fewer pages, but for the time being, with PR frequency going up and outages also increasing, pages for most teams are also going up.

The incidents that reach engineers will be the hard ones. The incidents that engineers are good at mitigating, like rolling back a bad deploy or undoing a feature flag rollout, will also be easy for agents. So, what’s left are the gnarly incidents, the hard-to-resolve ones, and those where the AI SRE failed to come up with a mitigation.

Engineers will de-skill unless this is countered. “Easy” incidents will increasingly be handled by AI, so engineers won’t be able to put the “reps” in to become competent incident managers. Sylvain Kalache, who runs Rootly AI Labs said:

“If you want to be the best tennis player, you can watch the games, but you are never going to learn to play tennis by only doing this! The same for software engineering, same for incident management. So, being in the hot seat and practicing these skills is very important.”

To avoid de-skilling, Rootly has created ‘Rootly Academy’, a setup to simulate incidents in Slack, using multiple AI personas, with the engineer playing incident manager. And Uptime Labs – an incident management startup – offers science-backed incident response training simulations. It turns out AI can be used as an educational tool for incident management as well.

Postmortems may no longer be big learning opportunities for engineers. Writing a postmortem after an incident used to be when a lot of learning took place. However, engineers don’t really enjoy this process, and naturally, all three AI SRE vendors draft postmortems with AI. Rootly told us that AI-drafted postmortems more than doubled between May and September this year, and 81% of them include at least one section generated by Rootly AI.

Engineers may not learn much from postmortems in the future, but AI SRE systems may start to use postmortems to further improve their investigation and root cause analysis skills.

Oncall engineers still can’t count on a full night’s sleep. That demo at Microsoft BUILD in 2025 mentioned at the top of this article was somewhat “smoke and mirrors”, and we can confirm that engineers sleeping while autonomous agents fix production issues is still out of reach, as yet. It’s true that AI agents have greatly improved, but for systems where downtime costs money, users, and credibility, agents are still considered too risky to be given full control of production systems.

Takeaways

Gergely, again.

It feels like code reviews and oncall are trending in the same direction: AI agents will take on “trivial”, low-risk stuff, and engineers will keep being involved in more risky decisions.

There’s an interesting parallel between deployments and oncall with AI: engineers still approve code pushed to prod, as well as AI agent actions during an outage. I don’t know of any major company shipping code to production on any important systems, as a bad deploy could cause an outage, data loss, and so on. During an outage, the last thing you want is to make things worse with an AI SRE making bad calls.

The AI SRE category will be competitive. For an AI SRE to be efficient, it needs context: the more context, the better! Due to this, companies will start to offer AI SRE solutions:

  • AI SRE startups: Rootly, incident.io, and ResolveAI are in this category, as are many others. It’s a segment with lots of growth opportunities, so raising venture funding is an option.

  • Observability companies: they already have telemetry, monitoring, and logging, which is the context an AI SRE needs. Many of these vendors have launched their own AI SRE solutions that build on top of their systems.

  • Coding harnesses: in-house coding harnesses like at Monzo already do AI SRE work, so it’s logical that coding harness vendors start to offer some kind of AI SRE

  • In-house solutions: in-house AI SREs could have access to more higher-quality context, especially at large companies. With an in-house agent, you can safely give it access to more sensitive information

The “deskilling” of oncall engineers may start to hurt. Dealing with complex incidents is always a challenge as they’re stressful, and experience of similar situations comes in handy. But what happens when engineers are inexperienced because they never get paged about “trivial” mitigations?

When I worked at Uber, the company had a special oncall group called Ring0, which was a group of select engineers and SREs who responded to the highest severity outages. To join, engineers needed to take in-house oncall training, shadow a sufficient number of outages, and take part in outage simulation training every 6-12 months.

I predict that AI will shield engineers from simple outages, meaning they get less practice to build up the skills for when a complex outage happens. Perhaps we can use AI to craft simulations of complex outages, and “upskill” oncall engineers like that.

What are you seeing of AI SRE tools at your company, and what about training for oncall and incident management? Do leave a comment!

How Apple Fits an LLM on Your iPhone

ByteByteGo
Oct 27
 
READ IN APP
 

[Webinar] How to stop rewriting your agent’s code (Sponsored)

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

Join us live on Oct 28 (FREE) to see:

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

Register now

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network. You can use it to process and generate language. How the model behaves is dependent on the numerical values you teach it during training. These numerical values are known as parameters.

Apple fits a 3-billion-parameter model on your iPhone. What this means is that the model has roughly 3 billion numerical values that it needs to work properly. These values influence how the model makes sense of its input and how it produces output.

How is Apple able to fit such a model on an iPhone without any adverse impact on the device?

In this article, we’ll try to answer this question. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The problems of running an LLM on a phone

  • How Apple makes the weights cheaper to store

  • How Apple made repeated calculations faster

  • How adapters help features share the foundation

  • How Apple optimizes the hardware to run the models

  • How does the system decide when to use the cloud

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Problems of Running an LLM on a Phone

Running an LLM is also called inference. In this stage, the LLM uses its parameters to process a request.

Before processing some text, the LLM has to divide it into tokens. You can think of a token as a word, part of a word, or even punctuation. The model takes these tokens and generates more tokens as part of the response. Within the model, these tokens pass through a bunch of processing layers.

The first problem is about storing the parameters.

At 16-bit precision, the 3 billion parameters we talked about earlier can occupy almost 6GB. But that’s not all. You need space for the input prompt, calculations, and temporary results that the model needs. Lastly, you also need to run the OS and other apps using the same memory. As you can see, storage is a big decision.

The second problem is about moving the weights quickly from memory to the processor. During text generation, the processor has to repeatedly fetch numerical data from memory. Even if you have a powerful processor, it might spend a lot of time just waiting for that data to be fetched from memory.

The Apple engineering team also had to deal with the challenges regarding memory capacity and memory bandwidth while trying to make their LLM run on the iPhone. On top of this, a mobile phone also has to take care of battery consumption, overheating, and other apps trying to use the same resources. You don’t want the LLM to make the rest of the device unresponsive.

How Apple Makes the Weights Cheaper to Store

The most direct way of reducing the size of the model is to use fewer bits to store each weight. This technique is known as quantization.

You can think of quantization as a way to represent numerical values using a smaller set of possibilities. Sure, you lose some numerical detail in the process. But the model can still perform its tasks at a pretty good level. The main trade-off is to select a representation approach that sits at the sweet spot for memory savings and quality. See the diagram below.

The Apple engineering team uses a technique known as palettization. In this technique, you group similar weight values. A small lookup table stores representative values, and individual weights store short references to that table. For example, you can have a 2-bit reference select from four entries in a lookup table.

In the earlier model version, the Apple engineering team combined 2-bit and 4-bit representations. It has an average of 3.7 bits per weight. This meant that the 3 billion weights could be stored in approximately 1.39 GB. A pretty good optimization.

They mixed different precisions because different parts of a model can easily handle different amounts of numerical error. You need to spend more bits on sensitive components so that quality doesn’t go down. Other components can be compressed more.

The later model Apple released makes the compression even more aggressive. The main decoder weights use 2 bits per weight. The embedding table uses 4 bits per weight. To make this compression work, Apple uses quantization-aware training. In this approach, you simulate the kind of restrictions that quantization will impose. Then, you adjust the model’s weights with those restrictions in place so that it can learn to work under them.

How Apple Made Repeated Calculations Faster

The weight storage is only one part of the overall memory problem. After you have successfully compressed the model, the model still needs memory to process a request.

Let’s say you have a model that has already read a paragraph of text and generated the beginning of a response. When the model tries to predict the next token, it needs to use information from earlier tokens. However, if you have to recalculate every intermediate result, it would be a big waste of computational resources.

A KV cache (key-value cache) stores these intermediate results. You can think of this cache as a way to reuse calculations that have already been done. However, the KV cache has a trade-off. As you can see, the cache takes up memory. The more text you have in a request, the more information you need to store in the cache. Even if you have a model whose weights fit comfortably within the memory, it can still face memory issues when processing a document with lots of text.

This means you have two targets to optimize. First, you can compress weights to reduce the space required by the model. Second, you can try to reduce the size of the KV cache.

Apple performs the cache optimization through a technique known as cross-layer KV sharing. In this technique, you need to divide the model into two blocks with a 5:3 depth ratio. Layers in the second block reuse keys and values produced by the final layer of the first block. By using this approach, Apple has brought down the KV-cache memory usage by 37.5%.

How Adapters Help Features Share the Foundation

You can use compression to reduce the size and cost of one model. But often, you may need many copies of that model with slightly different capabilities.

A simple approach would be to create one model for summarization. One for rewriting. Another for extracting information. And so on. But all these models would have a great deal of overlapping language capability. You are basically duplicating all of that capability.

An adapter can help you get rid of this duplication. You can think of an adapter as a small collection of parameters that changes how a base model works for a specific task. For example, let’s say you have a feature that writes concise notification summaries. Another rewrites longer passages into a different style. Both of these features can share the same base LLM. No need for duplication.

This technique is known as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation). While training an adapter, you fix the base model’s weights. Only the adapter weights are modified. This is why it becomes cheaper to specialize a model as compared to distributing a separate new model.

Apple applies adapters to various features such as attention matrices, attention-output projections, and feed-forward layers. Its rank-16 adapters use 16-bit values and occupy approx tens of MBs. They can load, cache, or swap these adapters as needed.

How Apple Optimizes the Hardware Running the Model

Even if the model is small, you need an efficient hardware implementation to run the model at the best of its ability.

Apple iPhones have several kinds of processors to take care of this. You have the CPU that handles all the general-purpose work. Then, you have the GPU that can deal with many numerical operations in parallel. The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) can run machine-learning workloads efficiently.

However, you can’t just use an accelerator and think that the model will run efficiently. You still need to select the right data layouts and split large arrays into manageable pieces. Also, you need to minimize memory copies. These techniques have an impact on speed as well as memory use.

How Does the System Decide When to Use the Cloud

Even after making all these optimizations, the model has limits.

In the case of Apple, its on-device model is quite capable of tasks like summarization, extraction, and classification. However, Apple Intelligence checks whether a request can be processed on the device. However, for more complex work, it can send the request to Private Cloud Compute (PCC).

PCC gives you a protected environment within which only authorized software can process the data. It also restricts any external parties from seeing the data.

Apple uses an encrypted network connection to protect information as it travels to the cloud. Your device encrypts the request for validated PCC nodes. Any infrastructure that is outside this boundary doesn’t have the keys to decrypt the request and read its contents. The data can be read only when it crosses into the authorized boundary. The goal is to make sure that even Apple’s staff and admin systems cannot access what’s inside this request.

When the request finally reaches the cloud, a separate server model takes care of the request. Apple uses mixture-of-experts computation and parallel processing tracks. This lets a large model choose the best computational components to distribute work.

Conclusion

Apple has been making a lot of new changes to its model.

In 2026, they launched the AFM 3 Core. It’s a new generation of its 3-billion-parameter model. Also, AFM 3 Core Advanced. It’s a sparse model with 20 billion total parameters. But it activates only 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time, based on the capabilities of the Apple Silicon systems.

In Core Advanced, the full model is stored on flash storage. Only expert weights are loaded into RAM. It selects weights based on the prompt. No need to change experts from the flash drive for every token. Apple has also expanded the cloud architecture. You can now run PCC workloads on NVIDIA GPUs in Google Cloud.

The main design principle that Apple follows is that the model’s capability should be based on the resources that are available at runtime. All of the techniques we’ve looked at come together to give the best experience to the users.

References:

  • Apple ML Research: Introducing Foundation Models

  • Apple ML Research: 2025 Updates

  • Apple Security Research: Private Cloud Compute

Mike Fisher

Somewhere right now, a 33-year-old with a decade of hard-won judgment is deciding the window has closed, while the data says they are still twelve years younger than the average founder of a top-performing company. Somewhere a team is killing a sound strategy in year two because someone sold it as a year-one story. The trap pushes a few people to fake success. It pushes far more to quit real success in progress because it’s arriving on an unfashionable schedule.”

Last chance to get every live course in one membership

Alex Xu
Oct 26
 
READ IN APP
 

We’ll stop selling ByteByteGo Live annual memberships on October 28 at 2 PM PT. After that, courses will be sold individually.

I wanted to explain why, and give you a chance to join before the change.

When we launched ByteByteGo Live (our cohort-based learning platform), we thought one membership covering every live course would make learning from industry experts simpler and more affordable.

But the membership offer has caused confusion. The enrollment has been lower than we hoped. So we’re simplifying things: choose the course you want to take, and pay for that course only.

For the next two days, you can still purchase the annual membership.

From the day you join, you can enroll in every live course we offer. Our current lineup includes:

  • AI Cost Optimization, taught by Jeremy Hintz, Engineering Lead at Meta.

  • Build Production Grade AI Systems, taught by Tanya Roosta, Director of AI at AMD.

  • AI Engineering Fundamentals, taught by Ali Aminian, bestselling author of books on machine learning and generative AI and contributor to AI courses at Stanford.

  • Build with Claude Code, taught by John Kim, Senior Staff Engineer at Meta.

  • AI Evals in Practice: For Engineers & PMs, taught by Manjeet Singh, Senior Director of AI Product Management at Salesforce.

  • Trust-optimized AI Development, taught by Kent Beck, creator of Extreme Programming and pioneer of test-driven development.

  • Rebuild YouTube with AI, taught by Mikhail Sychev, former YouTube tech lead at Google.

You’ll also get access to every new live course we add during your 12-month membership.

The annual membership is 78% below the combined listed value of our current courses.

Existing memberships, including those purchased before the cutoff, will keep the same access and benefits for their membership term.

If you are ready to build and ship real AI projects before the end of 2026, join now to access every live course.

Membership sales close on October 28 at 2 PM PT.

Get the ByteByteGo Live Membership →

This change only affects our live, cohort-based courses. Your ByteByteGo newsletter subscription isn’t changing.

Thank you for learning with us.

Alex Xu
Co-founder, ByteByteGo
